Encouraged by positive macroeconomic results and our determination to reach higher middle income status, We are now entering a decisive phase. For the period 2027 to 2030, we will accelerate implementation of the Emerging Comoros Plan. And we invite our bilateral and multilateral partners as well as the private sector, to join us in transforming this ambition into a lasting reality for the Comorian people. Mr. President, I would like to also express my deep gratitude for the inscription during the most recent session of the World Heritage Committee in Busan of six medinas of the historic Comorian sultanates, on UNESCO's World Heritage List. This historic recognition is the fruit of 20 years of work and it honors our nation. I would like to express our gratitude to all of the partners who helped us technically and financially and ultimately made this possible. Furthermore, our country in one year's time, the Union of the Comoros will host for the first time in its history, the Indian Ocean Islands Games. This major youth sporting event promotes cohesion and personal development in a world far too often marked by division and rejection of diversity. And here I would like to, on behalf of the Comorian people, I would like to thank all of the countries and partners whose support has helped make this national and regional undertaking possible. We intend to

make this event a resounding success. Mr. President, in conclusion, I call for ambitious action to restore confidence amongst our nations and do it through fairness, justice and solidarity. Let us transform the United Nations, our common home, into a more credible organization, and a source of hope for the future. It is only then that we will truly empower ourselves to act in all humanity, for humanity, in all of its differences and diversity. I thank you.

Developing nations must not be left behind as mere consumers or algorithms designed elsewhere. We must be supported in building true digital sovereignty. We join calls abiding ethical norms and greater regulation of artificial intelligence, particularly in warfare. Innovation must protect human development, not automate human destruction. Reforming global governance, correcting historic injustice. Mr. President, 80 years of patience is enough. The time for structural reform is now. We want to do that while also preserving something that no economic growth can replace, and that is its people, its territory, and its extraordinary biological diversity. Ladies and gentlemen, Bolivia has one specific feature, which is also perhaps an opportunity. We are a country with a small population but with diversity, the Andes, the Altiplano, the Amazon. We make up 60% of the water that the Amazon receives comes from Bolivia, one of the greatest cultural wealths of the continent and the world, and not just from one culture, many cultures within a single nation. And we have strategic natural resources which could be important for the energy and technological transition for the world. Each of the cell phones, the mobile phones that you have here in the room today, 10% of the tin that is in those cell phones comes from Bolivian tin. We have the capacity to provide the world with the resources that it needs to be able to develop a better world. Bolivia does not want to repeat the history of countries that exported their natural resources for decades and remained poor. We do not simply want to extract minerals from the earth so that other countries can add value to them. The ideology, and this is very important, I spoke earlier about organized crime and the mafia. In Bolivia, we have discovered and we are telling the world, the ideology of corruption is part and parcel of the destruction of knowledge, technology, research, infrastructure. and knowing how to properly make use of capital. The ideology of corruption runs counter to development. It runs counter to our democracies. For that reason, we must overthrow the ideological concept of corruption. We want partners that understand that an investment is not just a transfer of funds, of money. We want a long-term relationship with jobs, training, technology, infrastructure, productivity, a future. That is why Bolivia is open to the world and we want the world to come to Bolivia. But we are open with dignity. not based on demagogical speeches based on our past. What Bolivia wants is a firm and strong future, respecting our traditions and our original and indigenous peoples, but also giving them opportunities to grow with dignity and to develop our nations. Bolivia wants to enter partnerships, to compete, to learn, and it is also open to contributing. This historic moment has seen a discussion that we can no longer postpone. the transition to energy diversification. It's not so much a transition in and of itself, but rather diversifying our energy. The world needs cleaner energy sources, but it also needs minerals, lithium, copper, other critical minerals. It needs new supply chains and it needs to do that in a responsible way. And Bolivia wants to be a part of that conversation. But we would like to raise a question. Can the global energy diversification really be just if the countries that possess strategic resources continue to primarily export them as raw materials? No. That is why we want to enter into partnerships and open ourselves up to the world, but as a society, as partners, and not just as a source of raw materials. The energy transition also needs to represent productive diversification. It should create opportunities for producing countries. It should generate local capacities, respect the environment. It should incorporate and include communities, and it should allow our young people to be actors in those new industries. That is why we are proposing a new international relationship around strategic resources, a relationship that is based on investment, knowledge, technology, and added value. The United Nations, well, Bolivia is a country with one of the greatest forest reserves in the world. In the last 10 years, we've gone from 57% of a territory which around in the world represented forest reserves to less than 50% of that. Reforestation and the environment should be a priority for us. In my country, there was a president who talked about the Pachamama, which is God on Earth, and nevertheless, for the last 20 years, they have been destroying it. I think the Pachamama has changed its opinion now. It wants to grow and it wants to be taken care of, but it also wants an answer for its original peoples, its indigenous peoples, and the peoples of this region so that they can benefit from this care shown to the Pachamama. Bolivia cannot ask the world to protect our forests if we don't do our fair share as well. That is why we have already implemented various laws and norms which will be part of what Bolivia does among itself and with the world. The protection of the Amazon is a national responsibility, but it is also an international one. We want to conserve the Amazon. And for that reason, with neighboring countries that make up that Amazon region, we need to reach agreements. We cannot allow continued predating predatory activities on our Amazon, which is the lung of the world. Ladies and gentlemen, there are other challenges which I believe to be inseparable from the future of our nations. The fight against organized crime, as I have already said, organized crime has various different sources of financing. to finance myself, I had to ask multilaterals, I have to ask for resources that come late or sometimes never because the slow procedures that those multilateral organizations have mean that organized crime has an advantage when it comes to getting resources from drug trafficking, drug terrorism or the smuggling of gold to then destabilize our democracies. That is why multilateralism has to act much more immediately. It cannot be the case that one, two, or three billion dollars is the value of a democracy in crisis. Democracy is the priority in order to establish relations between our nations. The United Nations is built upon and based upon democracy, based upon respect for laws and having clear laws, having constitutions. But we have suffered from the attack of these narco-terrorists for 53 days again now. We have used dialogue and the technique and technology of peace. They wanted confrontation, they wanted blood on the streets. We instead offered dialogue and the technique of peace. And that same technique of peace, which I ask countries at war to use to end confrontations. Because when there is war in the world, those that suffer the most are the poor. When there is war in the world, it is the poor that suffer the most with fuel prices, energy, the cost of living. I'm welcome for this opportunity for Bolivia to be with you and to express our concerns. I will conclude by talking about Ban and Santa Cruz, two departments, and Cochabamba as well, which in September, this is the anniversary of those nine departments. But I would also like to express my fond affection to young Bolivians. Young Bolivians, just like the young people in all of the nations of the United Nations, need to find the meaning and purpose of their lives. Our nations need to give our young people that purpose. There will be the United Nations, Bolivia and countries in the future if we give that meaning to our young people, a meaning and a purpose in their lives, the very reason for being. I am and I am here to be part of building a society. That is why in these difficult moments that we are experiencing now, we are working in particular to ensure that young people have a purpose. They want to build the fatherland. They want to build our nation and want to be part of the United Nations as a concept of United Nations so that we can cooperate, work together, and to be firm in that conviction to be able to carry out a form of transformation and bring change to our work as a nation. I believe we need to build a new agenda. An agenda of energy, critical minerals, industrialization, infrastructure, digitalization, water, biodiversity, food security, education, health, gender, science, technology, connectivity, and other things. A new agenda for humanity. And we must debate that and discuss it because changes, digitalization is changing things very rapidly and changing our ability to understand what is happening in our countries. I am the product of digitalization. I conducted my campaign on social networks alone. I didn't use campaign experts. I didn't use millions of dollars for my campaign. It was only networks. And that is why urgent responses are needed to the challenges facing our nation. Thank you very much for this opportunity given to Bolivia, Bolivia today in this assembly. As I said, not everything has been resolved. We're just getting started. But Bolivia will never be on its knees. It will always stand tall. It will always stand up and be ready to walk forward and move ahead. I would like to thank each of the departments in my homeland and tell you that Bolivia is the homeland that never abandons us. The United Nations should also be the space that never abandons our homelands. This is the space for consolidating our democracy. This is the place where we can consolidate them against organized crime. This is the place where we can strengthen them for development. We have agreed to be part of the Shield of the Americas, but we have also agreed to be part of the Santiago Agreement to ensure that our democracies have security and certainty. and to provide them with progress and with a future. We never give in. Long live the home and dammit. Long live Bolivia. Thank you, United Nations.

On behalf of the Assembly, I wish to thank the constitutional president of the Plurinational State of Bolivia. The Assembly will hear an address by His Excellency Andr s Balint Bak, President of Hungary. I request protocol to escort His Excellency and invite him to address the Assembly.

Mr. President, Mr. Secretary General, Excellencies, It is a special honor to address this Assembly on behalf of Hungary. I speak here to the nations of the world, but also to my fellow citizens watching at home. For much of my life, I served as a judge in Hungary and at the European Court of Human Rights. That work taught me a simple lesson. The law must apply even to those in power. This belief will guide me as president. I will protect the constitution, the freedom of our institutions, and the dignity of every Hungarian citizen. The state belongs to those who support the government, to those who oppose it, and to those who have lost trust in politics whatsoever. A new political majority must not become the new owner of the state. This April, the people of Hungary voted for democratic renewal. They expected more than a change of government. They expect public life to change, rule of law, a state that serves rather than controls, courts that decide without pressure, a press that challenges power, and public money that is used for public goods. There must be accountability for corruption and abuse of power, but there must be no revenge. Justice cannot become a political weapon. A democratic state cannot repair past wrongs by repeating them with new people in charge. The same law must apply to those who governed yesterday, those who govern today, and those who may govern tomorrow. A republic begins when power accepts its limits. That is the republic Hungary must now rebuild. Trust from our partners will not return because of an election or one speech. Hungary asked to be judged by what we do. We will be a reliable member of the European Union, a committed NATO ally, and an active member of the United Nations. These partnerships do not take away our freedom, they protect it. Hungary will defend its national interest, but it will do so as a partner. We believe that national interest and international cooperation do not have to stand against each other. For Hungarians, the reasons are part of our own history. Seventy years ago, The revolution of 1956 expressed our people's determination to govern themselves. Soviet tanks crushed that hope. Our appeals reached the United Nations, but the international community could not prevent our defeat. Many countries represented here opened their doors to Hungarians who fled their country after the revolution. We remember both the cost of losing our independence and the help that allowed our people to start again. Today, Ukraine is fighting to preserve its independence. Hungary condemns Russia's full-scale war of aggression as a violation of United Nations Charter and international law. We affirm Ukraine's right to self-defense its sovereignty and territorial integrity within its internationally recognized borders, and the right of its people to decide their own future. The freedom Hungarians demanded for themselves in 1956 is a freedom we must uphold for Ukrainians today. We remember those who have lost their lives in this war, and we want diplomacy to bring the killing to an end. But a lasting peace must respect Ukraine's sovereignty. If taking territory by force becomes an accepted way of settling disputes, every smaller country will have reasons to worry about its own future. The principles of the Charter therefore matter to all of us. Human suffering cannot wait for diplomacy to succeed. People in conflict need food, medicine, and protection now. Hungary will continue to provide humanitarian aid to people in danger, especially the most vulnerable. In the Middle East, we call for full respect for international humanitarian law and for aid to reach those who need it safely and without interruption. Israelis and Palestinians must be able to live in security and dignity. A lasting peace must give their families reasons to believe that their children can grow up without the fear that has marked so many lives. For people forced from their homes by war and/or persecution, protection may first mean finding safety in another country. Hungary's own history gives us reason to understand that need. At the same time, every state has the right to protect its borders. Hungary will do so in accordance with international law. We will fight illegal migration and the criminal networks that profit from it by respecting human dignity and the protection given to refugees. But security is not only about borders and war. People also need the chance to build the future where they live. They need homes, schools, health care, and ways to earn a living. Poverty and the lack of opportunity can drive people from their countries just as conflict can. Hungary will continue to support development that helps communities build that future based on their own needs and priorities. We are ready to share our experience in education, health, and digital development. Water is another area where our interests meet. Drought can destroy crops, threaten food and energy supplies, and take away people's income. Climate change is making these pressures greater. Rivers also cross borders. What one country does can affect the water available to another. This makes cooperation essential. Hungary has experience in water management, sustainable agriculture, and climate adaptation, and we are ready to share it. For many countries represented in this hall, food, Energy, education, health, and jobs are immediate concern. We must give these issues to the same serious attention that we ask others to give European security. International cooperation works best when it responds to people's real needs and when every country has a voice. Excellencies, the United Nations faces a crisis of trust. Too often, it fails to act when powerful states and their friends break the rules. No country should be above the law. We cannot have one rule for our friends and another for others. But the answer is not to turn away from the United Nations. We need it, and we need it to work. It must be able to act treat all its members fairly, and apply the same principles to everyone. Hungary is ready to do its part. We will stand for human rights, support peacekeeping, and work with countries across the world to protect people and help diplomacy succeed. We must also look beyond the problems today. Many of the decisions we make now will shape the lives of people who are not yet born. A school, a strong institution, or a safe water system can benefit people for many years. Future generations must therefore have a place in the decisions we make today. Hungary supports stronger international action to protect their interest. including the appointment of a United Nations special envoy for future generations. The United Nations cannot demand trust. It must earn it. The same is true of every state and every public institution. The Hungarian people have asked us to restore their confidence in the future. We will honor that choice by rebuilding trust at home and by becoming a country others can trust when their own future is at stake. For Hungary, this is a new beginning, but the principle behind is not new. Power earns trust only when it accepts law. That is the responsibility Hungary accepts and the work we are ready to undertake with you. Thank you very much for your attention.

On behalf of the Assembly, I wish to thank the President of Hungary. The Assembly will hear an address by His Excellency Yamandu Orsi, President of the Oriental Republic of Uruguay. I request protocol to escort His Excellency and invite him to address the Assembly.

Mr. President of the General Assembly, Mr. Secretary-General, Heads of State, ladies and gentlemen. It is fitting that I begin by paying tribute to the people of the United States who 250 years ago, a quarter of a millennium ago, decided and understood that people have rights, the right to life, to their liberty and to happiness, and that these rights should guide every government, and that it is the governed who should decide who should govern them. We in South America, also peoples of migrants inherited these same principles 50 years on. And to that we say, cheers. I appear before this Assembly on behalf of a young country, but one with deeply rooted traditions. A country that over the course of its history has learned that governing doesn't merely mean administering resources or institutions. Above all, it means working for the well-being of people. And that has been one of Uruguay's great purposes, building a society in which dignity, freedom, peaceful coexistence and opportunities can be a part of people's everyday lives. And if there is one word that sums up much of our vocation as a country, that word would be peace. We do not view peace simply as an absence of war. We understand it as something that has to be constantly built. the possibility for people to live, to work, to educate their children, pursue their aspirations and to look to the future without fear. Uruguay, with its virtues, but also like every country with its darker times, has been a country that has sought to resolve its differences through institutions, through dialogue and through the quest for agreement. In this Assembly, we reaffirm our enduring willingness to contribute to peacekeeping missions with a deep sense of responsibility and solidarity. Uruguayan men and women can bear witness to the value of this instrument in easing suffering and guaranteeing respect for the human lives of the most defenseless populations. You can continue to count on Uruguay here. We are not a country given to grand gestures. We are a country of deeply held beliefs. And one of these beliefs is that peacebuilding is never finished. We can't take it for granted. Every generation has the responsibility to build it anew. There can't be peace for some and another peace for others. No suffering matters more because it happens closer to home and no lives are worth less because they were born in another country. When people suffer, humanity as a whole bears a responsibility. When a people is displaced, when a family loses its home, when young people can see no way out and their mental health is under threat, When a child grows up under the sound of gunfire, when millions of people live in poverty or without any opportunities, we can't stand indifferent to that. Nor can we stand indifferent to the pain caused by a state of endless war, the fear and pain generated by organized crime or the constant threat of terrorism, the repression born out of tyranny or the suffering triggered by a rigid economic blockade such as that endured by the Cuban people. We don't believe that taking one side or another in a war, confrontation or dispute necessarily contributes to resolving it. Indeed, very often it only serves to further the divisions. We have a different commitment, that is to seek path towards understanding, to open spaces for dialogue and to help to ensure that conflicts find a peaceful resolution. This doesn't mean indifference. It doesn't mean downplaying suffering. It doesn't mean overlooking responsibilities. It means understanding that peace demands something more difficult than merely taking sides. It means that we need to work so that that confrontation can be brought to an end as soon as possible. And to do that, we also have to recover something that at times seems to have been lost in international debate, humility. Uruguayans have an expression that sums up an understanding of coexistence. No one is better than anyone else. No country holds the absolute truth. No nation has a monopoly on their solutions. No society can claim that its historical experience is universal. And no people should be doomed to choose between models imposed from outside. Our understanding of relations among countries stems from that notion of humility. This is a humility that doesn't mean weakness. On the contrary, it means recognizing our own limitations while at the same time trusting in the abilities of others. We come from a country that is diverse in its opinions, but one that is deeply committed to the possibility of building a common future. And we believe that this combination, diversity of ideas and cohesion around the future, can also serve as our contribution to the international community. Today, we are living through a particularly difficult period. Extreme inequality remains one of the great threats to coexistence. Poverty continues to deprive millions of people of basic opportunities and wars continue to destroy lives, communities and hopes. While we discuss growth, technology, artificial intelligence, the energy transition or new forms of production, there are millions of people who continue to ask themselves far more basic questions. How will I feed my children? How can I find housing? How can I find a job? Or how can I face tomorrow without fear? We mustn't lose sight of that reality. Development makes sense when it improves people's lives. Economies make sense when they serve society. Technology makes sense when it expands our freedoms and opportunities. and politics makes sense when it is able to transform reality to bring happiness to our people. We are speaking from the experience of a small country removed from the great centres of power. However, we are convinced that our size shouldn't determine our ability to contribute, much less affect our own dignity. We need more effective, more representative multilateral institutions that are closer to the people and more able to respond to the challenges of our time. We need cooperation, we need solidarity and we also need to demonstrate austerity within these institutions. But above all We need to restore trust in our collective ability to change things because at its heart, the very idea of well-being and progress springs from something that is profoundly human, that is the ability to recognize suffering and refuse to accept inertia. Human beings are creative precisely because they refuse to resign themselves to things they sense what causes pain. They sense what could be different and then they're able to sense the desire for change. And this desire for change is perhaps one of the most profound expressions of our own freedom. When our peoples advance along the path of progress, they generally do so by wielding the powerful magic of freedom. Knowing that freedom doesn't come involve solely choosing between different possibilities. It also means being able to transform those things that we wish to for the good of the community as a whole. Our freedom becomes fuller when we are able to expand the freedom of others, when we change our societies through dialogue, when we build fairer institutions, when we undertake significant projects that endure beyond our own lifetimes. When school, a new school opens its doors, when a child has an opportunity that was previously out of their reach, when a community is able to overcome a division, when two countries that were at odds finally find a path towards understanding. Today, there are more than 8 billion people living on the same planet. 8 billion different stories, 8 billion hopes, 8 billion possibilities. We are not finished as such as humanity. We are a humanity still in the making. Every morning we have the chance to decide what kind of world we want to leave to those who come after us. We can choose to accept inequality as inevitable. We could accept war as something permanent, accept poverty as our fate. We could accept mistrust replacing dialogue. Or, on the contrary, we could choose another path, the most difficult path, but also the most human one. Uruguay, therefore, comes before this Assembly today with that belief, with the humility and respect of a small country but also with the resolve of those who understand the value of their principles. We've come to say that peace is no utopia. It is an ongoing endeavor. No conflict is ever definitively resolved through more conflict. No society becomes safer when hopelessness becomes the norm. No country can build its well-being in isolation. The future of humanity will, to a large extent, depend on our ability to understand that we are profoundly interconnected. We are different. We think differently. We have different histories. We have different interests. We are well aware that this isn't a struggle between the good guys and the bad guys. All too often, the good guys quickly become the bad guys. or those that we harshly condemned yesterday magically become the standard bearers of our alliance for good. But we share the same planet and ultimately the same destiny. Every day the UN has an increasing reason to exist and it must inevitably evolve in step with the geopolitical changes unfolding at dizzy

in speed. Every nation within this organization must play an active role within it, each to the fullest extent of their capacities. It's clear that our efforts should focus on ensuring that this is an up-to-date organization, properly supported, taking fair decisions that are respected. Countries' borders cannot be subject to human whims. They must be protected and respected as they represent the boundaries established to preserve identity, distinctive character, and a sense of belonging of their respective populations. We cannot continue to be held hostage to the will of a handful of countries that can be counted on the fingers of one hand, nor can we yield to the economic expediencies of the time. The aim here is clear, to achieve lasting stability, to ensure that the efforts of our citizens and their governments are channeled towards generating prosperity, far removed, of course, from the destruction and suffering caused by war. And we have made a commitment. Let us honor it right now. The history that ultimately prevails will be the history that we write every day through our action. For all of these reasons, Uruguay will continue to support dialogue, multi-naturalism, cooperation, international law, and the peaceful settlement of disputes, and above all, for the dignity of every human being. Humanity continues to refuse to regard itself as definitively complete, and perhaps that's our greatest hope. The hope that we can still change, that we can still learn, that we can still build, and that we can still choose peace. And this mere fact ultimately reminds us of the clear purity of the idea that together we stand and together we change. Little is contributed to the purposes of the UN by merely using this rostrum to accuse or attack. fire, the fire doesn't need any more fuel. Let us better harness this opportunity and let us give peace another chance. Because relations among states, just like relations between good people, bring happiness if we refrain from trading blows or elbowing one another aside. Thank you very much.

On behalf of the Assembly, I wish to thank the President of the Oriental Republic of Uruguay. We shall now continue the general debate. The Assembly will hear an address by His Excellency Antonio Costa, President of the European Council of the European Union. I request protocol to escort His Excellency and invite him to address the Assembly.

Mr. President of the General Assembly, Secretary-General, Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, multilateralism is not an ideal of the past. It is the only realistic way to address the problems of today. Alone, no country can prevent a pandemic, stabilize the climate, secure resilient supply chains, regulate artificial intelligence, ensure financial stability, or deliver sustainable development. Alone, no country, however powerful, can build lasting peace. And this is why Our message is clear. We need multilateralism, multilateralism that is strong, effective, representative, and capable of delivering for people. Multilateralism that protects human rights, strengthens democracy, and advances gender equality. Multilateralism equipped to address the defining challenges of today, peace, the climate emergency, economic insecurity, and artificial intelligence. On artificial intelligence and its governance, we need an accountable, transparent, and regulated architecture. We need an AI that serves humanity, not controls it. We must always be in the driving seat, setting a safe and secure pace of innovation and development. The artificial intelligence industry cannot be regulated by a few major global companies. And the United Nations must play a central role in setting global standards through the United Nations Global Digital Compact, the Independent International Scientific Panel, and the Global Dialogue on AI Governance. Excellencies, The United Nations must remain at the center of the multilateral system. The United Nations is under pressure from geopolitical polarization, financial constraints, and institution shortcomings. But the answer is not withdrawal. The answer is to reform, renew, and reinvest. The UN80 initiative offers an opportunity to make the United Nations more efficient and more effective. The European Union also continues to call for a comprehensive reform of the United Nations Security Council to make it more effective, inclusive, democratic and accountable. The European Union will continue to contribute to strengthen the United Nations politically, financially and through concrete actions. Because the best argument for multilateralism is what it delivers on peace and security with the Treaty of Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons, on climate action with the Paris Agreement, on poverty and health with the global response to COVID-19. The truth is, when we act together, multilateralism delivers for people. And this is why this week, the United Union, the European Union has launched together with Australia, Barbados, Brazil, Canada, India, and Kenya, the P4M, Partners for Multilateralism, International Law, Peace, and Prosperity. Our initiative aims to be an open platform for partners from all parts of the world who are ready to defend common principles and work towards practical solutions. It is a network for dialogue, coalition building, and practical cooperation. It will support the work of United Nations and other multilateral formats. It will help to build bridges across regions, and it will contribute to advancing the reform and modernization of the United Nations and the multilateral system, helping to turn shared commitments into concrete action. And I invite all the nations in this chamber to join this initiative and endorse the P4M declarations. Excellences.

There can be no double standards in terms of international law. The facts are clear. We are bearing witness to deliberate violations of international law. Following and defending international law is not an option. It is our responsibility. That means protecting the institutions that give their very meaning to these principles, including the International Court of Justice and the International Criminal Court. We support these courts firmly and we will defend their independence, integrity and their ability to fully carry out their mandate. Threats and attacks on the International Criminal Court and its staff and authorities are unacceptable. Accountability cannot depend on political considerations. International law applies everywhere. International humanitarian law applies everywhere and human rights apply everywhere in Ukraine, in the Middle East, in Africa, in Asia or in Latin America. We are well aware that conflicts never remain purely local. They have repercussions on food security, energy markets, immigration, development and global stability. We can see that with the war of aggression by Russia on Ukraine. This was a war chosen by Russia, the consequences of which are worldwide in scope. This is a devastating aggression on a sovereign state committed by a permanent member of the UN Security Council. The violation of the UN Charter and of international law attacks by Russia on Ukraine also threaten the security of civilian populations beyond Ukraine's borders, and it is unacceptable that over the last 12 months, Russia has on several occasions threatened the security of several European Union member states. Russia must bring an end to this dangerous escalation, and the international community must do its utmost and use all of the tools available to it to bring an end to this war and to create the conditions for negotiations for a comprehensive, just and lasting peace. This war must end. The same goes in the Middle East. We regret the current stalemate in Gaza and more broadly speaking in Palestine, which is prolonging the suffering of millions of civilians despite the momentum towards the end of the conflict that we thought we saw at the end of last year. The European Union and its member states have made their positions clear. The two state solution is the only one that can ensure lasting peace in the Middle East. with the State of Israel and the State of Palestine independent and living side by side in peace and security. And we also support all of the efforts to find a solution to the conflict in Iran. The ceasefire must be fully respected. Freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz must be preserved without conditions and without hindrance. For a lasting solution, it is also necessary that security of the countries in the region be ensured. It is essential that Iran never be allowed to acquire nuclear weapons. And finally, we hope that the Iranian people can in the future live in peace, security, and as free men and women. Excellencies, the United Nations need an ambitious leader that is firmly committed to the principles of its charter and respect of international law, as is currently being demonstrated by Antonio Guterres. Here, I would like to pay tribute to the Secretary-General His clear efforts in favor of respect of the United Nations Charter, the defense of human rights, reforming the global financial architecture, sustainable development, and decisive action in the face of climate change have all been a true beacon lighting our path, guiding our collective commitment. Thank you very much, Antonio Guterres. The next Secretary-General, the next Secretary-General must continue to fully mobilize all of the tools available to them to be able to prevent conflict, mediate crises, and build peace, particularly emphasizing the Middle East, Sudan, and Ukraine. This commitment will depend on the robustness of the multilateral system tomorrow. Ladies and gentlemen, A more robust multilateral system also calls for stronger partnerships. The EU doesn't purport to impose a model or influence. We aspire to build space for progress and growth together with partners from all regions around the world. For this reason, we continue to build the most dense network of trade agreements in the world, covering 84 countries from around the planet. In the last 12 months alone, we concluded negotiations and signed agreements with India, Australia, Philippines, Mercosur, Mexico, among others, benefiting billions of people. But the value of what we can do with our partners needs to go beyond trade. no sphere is more urgent than that of sustainable development. The 2030 agenda is at risk. The financing gap is growing, the climate crisis is worsening, geopolitical divisions are curbing progress. We need to continue to work to reform the global financial architecture. The European Union stands steadfastly committed to the Paris Agreement, the Pact for the Future and the Sustainable Development Goals funded in line with the Seville Commitment. The EU and its Member States together represent more than 40% of official development assistance at the global level and through our Global Gateway initiative, we are investing in all fields, connectivity, health, education and eradication of poverty. But we mustn't lose any more time. For this reason, the Sustainable Development Goals 2027 should be a turning point to pick up the pace, to correct the mistakes and to commit to 2030 and beyond that.

The European Union is clear about its choice. Cooperation over confrontation. Law over power. Partnership over isolation. Action over paralysis. We are ready to work together with all those who share this conviction. Let us reform. Let us renew. Let us reinvest. Let us act together. Thank you very much.

Mr. Khalilur Rahman, President of the General Assembly; Mr. Antonio Guterres, Secretary-General of the United Nations; Excellencies, Heads of State and Government and Heads of Delegation; Ladies and Gentlemen. I have the honor to take the floor before this General Assembly on behalf of and representing His Excellency Obiang Nguema Mbasogo, President of the Republic of Equatorial Guinea, to express to you his greetings of peace and the greetings of the people of Equatorial Guinea, and to reaffirm our support for and commitment to the Charter of the United Nations. Mr. President, The theme of this session is Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation: A United Nations that Delivers for All. This theme invites us to consider international cooperation in a world that is subject to profound challenges. For Equatorial Guinea, trust is strengthened when we fulfill commitments that have been made and decisions that have been adopted collectively, and when visible results can be produced. The countries of the global South need cooperation that preserves peace, that drives sustainable and inclusive growth, and that expands the ability of each state to build its own future. Therefore, 21st century cooperation should provide opportunities for the mobilization of financing to transform raw materials and to develop one's own knowledge and technologies. Excellencies, this vision is especially relevant for Africa, which needs investments that can allow it to develop local value chains, build infrastructure, advance industrialization, strengthen human capital, incorporate new technologies, and generate employment, especially for the continent's large youth population. A more productive and industrialized Africa will be a stronger partner to the benefit of all of those wanting to halt its immigration. Excellencies, when the 2030 Agenda was adopted, the world embraced its deeply human vision, eradicating poverty, protecting the planet, and making sure that all people can live with dignity, leaving no one behind. However, as we approach its end date, we are far from meeting its goals. Poverty persists, inequality is expanding, and climate change continues to rage. It is clear that we need an international financial architecture that facilitates productive investments, that takes into account the real vulnerabilities of developing countries, and supports the efforts of each nation. It is therefore urgent to implement the resolutions adopted at the conferences in Addis Ababa in 2015 and in Seville last year. Mr. President, development requires peace and stability. Equatorial Guinea defends dialogue, negotiation, mediation, and the peaceful settlement of disputes. Our own experience demonstrates this. Equatorial Guinea and the Gabonese Republic are a clear example of commitment to peaceful settlement because they submitted their territorial disputes to the International Court of Justice. We express our recognition and gratitude for the valuable support of the United Nations and the African Union in this in that process. In which we have shown that it is possible to preserve ties of friendship, cooperation and good neighborliness. At the same time, Equatorial Guinea has its doors wide open for investors and partners from around the world. We are an African country. in which you will find stability, tax advantages, opportunities and a partner that is prepared to build relationships of mutual benefit and shared profit. Mr. President, distinguished delegations, restoring trust means showing that working together produces results. And managing transformation means turning the challenges of our time into new opportunities. Africa brings together 54 United Nations member states and represents a fundamental share of the political and demographic reality of the 21st century. We must move towards a more balanced international community in which Africa participates fully in global decisions and strengthens its ability to lead its own development. Equatorial Guinea reaffirms the African common position as enshrined in the Ezulwini Consensus and the Sirt Declaration. which calls for two permanent seats with veto right for Africa, as well as two additional non-permanent seats on the Security Council. Mr. President, Excellencies, Ladies and Gentlemen, Respect for international law, sovereign equality, and friendship with all peoples is what guides Equatorial Guinea's foreign policy. On behalf of President Obiang Nguema Mbasogo, the government and the people of Equatorial Guinea, we express our gratitude to him. And it is in that regard that Equatorial Guinea will continue to contribute based on mutual respect, sovereign equality, and dialogue to turn our cooperation into development and opportunities for future generations. Thank you very much.

Mr. President, Dr. Khalilur Rahman, Excellency, Mr. Antonio Guterres, Secretary-General of the United Nations, justice, excellencies, head of state and government, heads of delegation, distinguished delegates, ladies and gentlemen. It is a distinct honor for me to address this assembly on behalf of his excellency, Mr. Adam Aboro, president of the Republic of the Gambia. I bring to this hall the warm greetings of the government and people of the Gambia together with our enduring friendship, solidarity, and goodwill to all nations represented here. Mister president, Allow me at the outset to congratulate you most warmly on your election as President of the 84th session of the General Assembly. The Gambia assures you of our full support and constructive cooperation as we guide our collective work under the timely theme you have chosen, restoring trust and managing transformation so that the United Nations can deliver for all. That theme speaks directly to the moment in which we meet. Permit me also to express our profound appreciation to your predecessor, Ms. Annalena Baerbock, for the dedication, dignity, and determination with which she presided over the 80th session of the General Assembly. I also wish to place on record the Gambia's appreciation for the Secretary-General, Mr. Antonio Guterres, and Deputy Secretary-General, Amina Mohammed, whose steady and principled leadership through years of compounding global crises, have done much to keep the flame of multilateral cooperation alive, even as the winds against it have grown fiercer. We wish them well as they complete their tenure at the end of this year. Mr. President, few institutions embody the principle of sovereign equality as visibly as this Assembly. Within these walls, differences in power, wealth and influence may shape the realities our nations confront, but they do not confer a greater claim to membership or participation. And perhaps more than anywhere else, this Assembly reminds us of a simple truth: our differences are real, but so is our interdependence. This is why this Organization was created with understanding that disputes must be resolved through dialogue, human dignity must be protected, and that nations must work together if development, peace, and human rights are to be sustained. In other words, that our common future required common institutions. Eight decades later, we must ask ourselves whether we have remained faithful to that insight. And perhaps more importantly, do we still trust one another enough to act on it? Because today, Mr. President, trust is being tested. Geopolitical divisions are widening. Wars have become more protracted with devastating humanitarian consequences. Respect for the United Nations Charter and international law is under visible strain, with developing countries facing intensifying debt burden, climate vulnerabilities, huge gaps between commitments made and implementation, and feeling of marginalization and inadequate representation in the global system. Therefore, the task before us is building stronger, better equipped, representative, responsive, and an effective multilateral system and global financial architecture that delivers for all nations and regions. Mr. President, the Gambia's own experience within this organization gives us grounds for optimism. We have seen within this very institution that multilateralism can still deliver. During the 80th session of the General Assembly, The Gambia had the honor of chairing the second committee at a time of profound disagreement over some of the most consequential economic and development issues before us. That experience reminded us that multilateralism does not require unanimity on every issue. It requires the willingness to remain at the table, to listen, negotiate, and courage to make compromise. Our experience demonstrates that in this period of deep disagreement, Progress remains possible when Member States approach negotiations with political will, mutual respect, and a shared sense of responsibility. Mr. President, the stakes are perhaps greatest in international peace and security, one of the foremost purposes for which this Organization was created. If diplomacy can bring countries together to find common ground on difficult questions on global development, then surely we can summon the same political courage to prevent conflicts, resolve wars, and build lasting peace. The Gambia speaks on this not merely from principle, but from experience. In 2017, our country stood at a moment of acute constitutional uncertainty. The democratic choice of the Gambian people faced a grave challenge. At that critical moment, the preventive diplomacy of the United Nations, working in partnership with the African Union and ECOWAS, help uphold the will of the Gambian people and support a peaceful democratic transition. We have not forgotten that solidarity. It taught us that preventive diplomacy is not an abstract concept. It is a practical instrument for preventing confrontation, creating space for dialogue, and protecting institutions. Sometimes it can change the course of a nation. That experience also gives us an obligation. If the international community could stand with the Gambia at a moment of fragility, then countries facing similar moments should be able to count on the same solidarity. Across the world, however, conflicts continue to destroy lives, displace populations, and reverse decades of development. Civilians bear the greatest cost, while humanitarian workers operate under increasingly dangerous conditions, and the resources available to respond to crises remain far below what is required. The protection of civilians Respect for international humanitarian law and humanitarian access are not political conveniences. They are legal obligations and expressions of our shared humanity. We need stronger early warning systems that enable us to act before crises escalate, timely mediation before positions become entrenched, and peacebuilding that addresses the conditions that allow conflict to take root. The question before us must therefore Not only we have to end the ongoing wars, but how to prevent the next war from beginning. Prevention should not have to wait for a crisis to become sufficiently destructive to attract international attention. It is infinitely less costly in human, political, and financial terms to prevent conflict than to manage its consequences after violence has begun. We therefore welcome the Secretary-General's continued good offices and in preventing diplomacy and call for these efforts to be matched with predictable and sustained resources. Mr. President, peace must be built and nurtured through institutions that command public confidence, societies in which trust can be restored and justice pursued, and a future in which women and young people have a meaningful voice and economic opportunity is within reach. The Gambia has experienced the value of peacebuilding firsthand. Since our democratic transition, this Peacebuilding Commission and the Secretary-General's Peacebuilding Fund have been steadfast partners in our nationally-led efforts to strengthen institutions, advance transitional justice, and consolidate peace. We therefore support a stronger and more responsive Peacebuilding Commission, adequately resourced to support countries emerging from conflict or navigating delicate political transitions. The implementation of the outcomes of the peacebuilding architecture review must translate into stronger prevention, greater national ownership, and closer coordination across the United Nations system. We also reaffirm our support for United Nations peacebuilding operations and pay tribute to the men and women who serve under the UN flag, including government, military, and police personnel who have contributed with distinction to international peace and security. Their safety and security must remain a priority alongside performance, accountability, and strict adherence to international law. Partnerships between the United Nations and regional organizations, particularly the African Union, must also be deepened with sustained and predictable funding. Mr. President, the ongoing conflict in Sudan remains a matter of profound concern to the Gambia, together with continued instability across part of the Sahel. It reminds us that peace cannot be separated from development and governance. The suffering of civilians in the affected conflict zones globally demands sustained international attention and renewed diplomatic efforts towards the escalation, dialogue, and a durable political settlement. In the Sahel and other conflict zones, our responses must be comprehensive and holistic. Security measures are necessary, but they must be accompanied by increased support for democratic governance institution building, education, job creation, development, and climate resilience. Mr. President, for millions of people around the world, poverty, lack of human rights, democratic governance, et cetera, continue to pose greater insecurity. The absence of education, healthcare, decent employment, and the loss of homes and livelihoods to climate change leave communities as vulnerable as conflict itself. Our understanding of security must therefore extend beyond the absence of war to include the conditions that allow people to live with dignity, opportunity, and hope. Mr. President, in the Gambia, this understanding has guided our democratic journey from 2017 to date. We have undertaken the difficult work of rebuilding institutions, strengthening the rule of law, expanding access to justice, and confronting the legacy of past human rights violations. Our transitional justice process continues through implementation of the recommendation of the Truth, Reconciliation, and Reparations Commission. We have strengthened institutional accountability, established the Special Prosecution Office to advance investigations and prosecution arising from the TRRC process. We are proud of the progress we have made, but we remain conscious that democracy is never a finished project and requires continuous institutional strengthening adherence to rule of law, constitutional order, dialogue, and consensus building on issues. On the 5th of December 2026, the Gambian people will again exercise their sovereign democratic right to choose their president. This will be another important milestone in our democratic journey, and we need the support of the international community in this regard. Our government is committed to ensuring that the elections are peaceful, transparent, credible and inclusive and conducted in accordance with our constitution, national laws, and democratic standards. This is the democratic party government remains committed to pursuing. A part in which institutions are strengthened, citizens are heard, differences are resolved peacefully, and democratic gains are consolidated for future generations. Mister President, on development, the government's recovery focused national development plan provides a framework for accelerating our social enemy transformation. We are investing in roads, energy, schools, healthcare, agriculture, and digital infrastructure, while promoting economic diversification, private sector investment, and value addition. We are expanding opportunities for women and young people, improving lives, and strengthening the human capital upon which our future depends. I seize this opportunity to thank all the bilateral and multilateral partners of The Gambia for your continuous support and partnership. The global economic environment remains particularly difficult for developing countries with decline official development assistance, high borrowing costs, disruptions in international trade, inflationary pressures, and food and energy insecurity, narrowing fiscal space, and threatening development gains. With only a few years remaining to achieve the 2030 agenda, the time for implementation is now. Following the Fourth International Conference on Financing for Development, We must translate the severe commitments to tangible action. Developing countries need greater access to affordable, long-term finance, meaningful reform of the multilateral development system, sustainable solutions to debt, stronger international tax cooperation, and decisive action against illicit financial flows. We also need stronger and more resilient supply chains, greater investment in productive capacity, and a global economic system that gives developing countries a fair opportunity to transform their economies. Trade must remain an engine of development, and developing countries must be enabled to participate more effectively in regional and global value chains. The above would enable developing countries to invest in education, health, agriculture, climate resilience, and other productive sectors to holistically address their interconnected challenges. Mr. President, Climate change presents another test of our collective credibility, and for the government, it is not a distant threat. Coastal erosion, changing rainfall patterns, pressure on water resources, food insecurity, and environmental degradation are already affecting our communities and livelihoods. However, we are responding with determination by investing in renewable energy, coastal resilience, mangrove restoration, disaster risk reduction, early warning systems, water security, and nature-based solution. National electricity access is at 90%, universal access targeted by the end of 2026. We are expanding our solar energy in schools and health facilities, modernizing our electric network, and advancing a 150-megawatt solar park. But we urge that our national ambition be supported by international action to make climate finance accessible, predictable, and adequate, including through the sustained implementation of the new collective quantified goal on climate finance and effective management to address loss and damage, build climate resilience, and a fairer international order in which those who have contributed least to the climate crisis are not left to bear the greatest burdens. Mr. President, artificial intelligence and emerging technologies offer extraordinary opportunities, but opportunity without inclusion can become another source of inequality. The digital divide must not become the next development divide. Developing countries must not remain passive consumers of technologies designed elsewhere. We need the capacity to participate in research, innovation, entrepreneurship, and global technology governance. Technology must serve humanity, and the governance of artificial intelligence must be inclusive responsible, and grounded international cooperation. This is particularly important for the world's least developed countries. As the Gambia prepares to assume greater leadership within the Global Coordination Bureau of the LDC group, we do so with a clear sense of responsibility. LDCs continue to face structural constraints, including limited productive capacity, high debt burdens, climate vulnerability, narrow export base, technological gaps, and restricted access to affordable finance. We will continue to advocate for full implementation of the Doha Program of Action. Mr. President, migration is another area where our collective response must be guided by human dignity and shared responsibility. Migration continues significantly to economic development, cultural exchange, and human progress. Yet, irregular migration continues to expose young people and vulnerable populations to exploitation, trafficking, abuse, and tragic loss of life. We must strengthen cooperation for safe, orderly, and regular migration, protect the rights and dignity of migrants, and expand lawful pathways for labor mobility, as well as invest in young people, women, education, health, and social protection to safeguard sustainable development and lasting peace. Mr. President, The government welcomes the call for the reform of United Nations. We recognize the constraints facing the organization was limited with limited resources and increasing demands. This notwithstanding, the reforms would strengthen the capacity of United Nations to serve its member states and the people of the world better, as well as correct the historical injustice that continues to prevail. We need to embark on reforms that strengthen delivery protects the universal character of the organization and enables developing countries to participate meaningfully in decisions that shape their future. Mr. President, the General Assembly's decision to move towards a convention on the prevention and punishment of crimes against humanity is an important contribution to addressing a longstanding gap in the international legal framework. The Gambia is proud of its leading role alongside Mexico in advancing this process through more than three years of patient negotiation. Our conviction is simple. The gravest crimes cannot be met with silence. Victims cannot be forgotten. Impunity cannot become an accepted feature of international relations. Prevention, accountability, and justice are indispensable to reconciliation, healing, and sustainable peace. The rule of law is one of the foundations upon which trust is built. The continued development of multilateral treaties and the entry into force of the agreement on the conservation and sustainable use of marine biological diversity of areas beyond national jurisdiction also demonstrate what is possible when states negotiate in good faith and perseverance. The Gambia commends Ghana for its historic resolution on declaration of trafficking of enslaved Africans and racialized chattel enslavement of Africans as the gravest crime against humanity and to go for the resolution on correcting the map at the General Assembly. Mr. President, our credibility is ultimately tested by how we respond to conflicts and crises that remain unresolved for years. The suffering of the Palestinian people remains a profound test of the credibility of the international system. The G7 reiterates its call for the protection of civilians, respect for international humanitarian law, and unhindered humanitarian assistance. We reaffirm the legitimate and inalienable rights of the Palestinian people, including their right to self-determination, membership of the United Nations, and our support for a just, comprehensive, and lasting two-state solution, with Israel and Palestine living side by side in peace, security, and dignity. Furthermore, the plight of the Rohingya people must also not disappear from the international agenda. The G7 reaffirms, remains committed to accountability, justice, and the protection of their fundamental rights and would continue to need the support of you all in this shared collective endeavor. On Cuba, we reiterate our longstanding call for an end to the economic, commercial, and financial sanctions. Dialogue, engagement, and cooperation remain important instruments for improving people's well-being and strengthening peaceful relations among nations. The Gambia also affirms its adherence to the One China policy and values its partnership with the People's Republic of China, including in development cooperation, infrastructure, South-South and triangular cooperation, and partnership. The leaders of our two countries have raised our bilateral relations to a strategic level, and we will continue to grow and deepen this important partnership. On the question of the Murukan Sahara, the Gambia supports sustained international efforts towards a peaceful resolution through the United Nations-led political process. We encourage all concerned parties to engage constructively and in good faith. The real initiatives of Moroccan autonomy, the Moroccan-Nigeria gas pipeline, the Atlantic African initiative, amongst others, have provided realistic pathways to finding a lasting political solution to the dispute over the Moroccan Sahara by giving people the development, human rights, security, and stability they need. Furthermore, the GAMMAY welcomes the Kingdom of Morocco's continuous commitment to the ceasefire, full cooperation with MINURSO, and also stakeholders all stakeholders in line with resolution 2797 and other relevant processes. We urge all stakeholders, i.e. Polisario, the Kingdom of Morocco, Algeria, and the Islamic Republic of Mauritania, to continue working on achieving a sustainable political solution to the conflict, and we support the various initiatives of the United Nations in this regard. Mr. President, in conclusion, the United Nations and the multilateral system continue to be challenged. but they remain the most reliable guarantor of our collective peace and security and proven mechanisms to confront the challenges facing humanity. Therefore, the task before us is to make the United Nations, the multilateral system, more responsive, more representative, and better able to deliver for the people that we serve. What we leave behind should be a legacy of renewed multilateralism, a reformed United Nations, increased international cooperation and solidarity, and an increased trusted global system that sustains peace, advances development, human rights, democracy, and opens the way to a more secure future for all. The Gambia stands ready to work with every member state to renew the promise that brought the nations of the world together. My country's own journey has taught us that countries and institutions can evolve from moments of profound uncertainty and further build and increase trust and confidence. This is the message that we bring to this Assembly. I thank you for your kind attention.

Mr. Secretary-General, Mr. Vice-President of the General Assembly, Heads of State and Government, Excellencies, Ambassadors, Ladies and Gentlemen, I appear today before this Assembly representing the President of the Republic of Colombia, Abelardo de la Espriella, who has asked me to be here on his behalf and bring before you a message written by him. From this moment on, what you will hear are the words of the President of the Republic of Colombia.

I have asked the Vice President of the Republic, Jose Manuel Restrepo, to read this message on my behalf. I have done so because I assured the Colombian people that I would not leave the country during the four years of my term, and I'm keeping that promise. 47 days ago, a new government took office in Colombia. 34 a.m. the earth shook. A 7.4 magnitude earthquake struck my country. In a matter of seconds, homes, hospitals, schools, roads and bridges had been totally destroyed or severely damaged. The Colombian Geological Service confirmed that this was the strongest magnitude earthquake recorded in Colombia so far this century. Hundreds of Colombians lost their lives. 4,500 were injured and more than 452,000 people were affected. 36,000 homes were totally destroyed. They represented the life savings assets of these people. The government that had barely started its work was forced to confront one of the greatest natural disasters in our recent history. There was no time to ask whether we were ready. We had to act, and we did so. From the very outset, I gave one unequivocal instruction. We had to save human lives. There was time for everything else. Appointments to posts could wait, meetings could wait, but my fellow Colombians trapped underneath the rubble could not. The government deployed to the affected areas alongside the security forces, emergency services, volunteers and rescue workers, and From the very beginning, we started receiving the generous assistance from friendly countries and international organizations, such as all of you. And today, from this rostrum, I wish to express the profound and sincere gratitude of the Colombian people to all of you. The earthquake claimed the lives of many of our fellow Colombians and destroyed thousands of homes, buildings and much infrastructure, but it also reminded us once again of something that Colombians are very familiar with. We might fall, we might suffer, we might weep, but what we cannot and what we do not know how to do is give up. But I'm not only going to talk to you about this tragedy. I want to refer to what Colombia decided to do in its aftermath. On the 7th of August, I took over a country that had begun to lose something far more difficult to rebuild than a road or a building, that is trust. Trust in the law that should protect our citizens, trust that working, studying and doing things well are worthwhile. trust in a state that lives up to its duty. No country, no country can prosper when its people cease to trust in it. That's why the government that I lead has tasked itself with taking up every possible decision to enable Colombia to believe in itself again and to ensure that the world can believe in Colombia again. And I call that overarching purpose the Patria Milagro, the miracle nation. The first step is a basic one, restoring security. For far too long, Colombians have had to live alongside situations that no society should accept as normal. A rural farmer having to ask permission from a terrorist group to work on his land. a shopkeeper having to hand over part of the fruits of his labor to extortionists, a mother increasingly gripped by fear every time their child goes out to play in the park. That is not and it cannot become the norm. Consequently, from the very beginning of my government, I gave the security forces one clear instruction. to regain territorial control, to fully restore the state's authority, and to confront the structures using terrorism. My government is determined to do away with euphemisms. Organizations that murder, that kidnap, that use explosives, that recruit children, and that deliberately resort to terror to subjugate a society are terrorist groups. That is what we call them. And we are facing up to them with the full legitimate force of the state within the constitution and within the law. But there is another reality that is very often overlooked. The illicit drugs produced in Colombia don't end up in Colombia. Drugs trafficking is a transnational Criminal enterprise, its root.

cross borders, its money moves through international financial systems and its networks operate across numerous countries. I will do everything necessary to combat that scourge, but a transnational threat requires the international community to play its part as well. Security, while essential, is not enough. A territory that provides no opportunities remains vulnerable. My administration is therefore also focused on ensuring that Colombia grows again. For years, we have discussed how to better distribute what we have. That is a legitimate, necessary discussion, but it's absolutely not enough. We also need to ask ourselves, how are we going to produce more? In the end, Governments can't decree economic growth. What they have to do is lay the foundations for it to occur. In our miracle nation, we want an idea to be able to become a business, a business to create jobs and for jobs to become well-being for our people. To those of you anywhere else in the world who are wondering where to invest, I would like to invite you to look at Colombia. It's a country with access to two oceans, productive land, energy resources, enormous biodiversity, an excellent geographical position, and a government that champions private enterprise. But above all, look at our people. Colombia does not want to watch the technological transformation of our time from the sidelines. We want to be a part of it. We want to train young people for super intelligence, for robotics, for data science, for agro industry, for engineering, and for the new economy. Millions of Colombians are not asking the state to sought out their lives, they're asking the state to give them the opportunity to build those lives. And that is what gives meaning to what I have called the miracle nation. This isn't the name of a government. nor is it a naive promise that our problems will just disappear. No, that's not it. This is the country that we're going to build. It's a country where security allows us to reclaim our territories threatened by terrorism, where trust attracts investment, where investment creates jobs, and where growth leads to better living conditions. It is a school teacher in Monpos, Bolivar, teaching with the tools of the 21st century. It is a rural farmer in Ubate, Cundinamarca, who can now sow, sell, and prosper thanks to his work. It's a young woman in Pasto, Nariino, preparing to be a part of the future industries. This is the miracle nation that we've already started to build. I am well aware that 47 days is far too little time to change a country, but it is enough time to change the course of a country. I want Colombia to once again enjoy strong growth. That growth should lead to a job for a young person, a home for a family, timely access to medicines, harvest that finds a market and Colombians who, thanks to their own efforts and dedication, can escape poverty. This is our miracle economy, an economy that grows so that people can grow with it. Our relationship with the world is also a part of this purpose. Over the last few weeks, we have seen this very tangibly when friendly countries and international organizations came to our aid following the earthquake. This solidarity makes full sense when it reaches people, when it solves problems, and when it produces results. and it is precisely because I recognize the value of that cooperation that today I want to speak frankly about the UN. I've been critical about this organization. I was critical of it before I became president and it would be inconsistent to address this assembly today and conceal my attempt to conceal my convictions. This criticism isn't born out of whim or hostility towards the United Nations, it's based in political, institutional, doctrinal considerations. I believe in the UN as an organization and it is precisely for that reason that I believe it's legitimate to ask whether the institutions that we've been building are effectively responding to the problems that that it was created to address. The charter itself is very clear here. This organization was born to maintain international peace and security, to foster friendly relations among nations, and to promote cooperation in resolving the major common problems. Eight decades on, the question cannot be whether those purposes remain valid. Of course they do. The questions have completely changed though. Is the UN fulfilling those purposes with the effectiveness demanded by today's world? Are there bureaucratic structures that have become excessively cumbersome? Are we dedicating too many resources, too much energy to administering procedures and or too little to resolving problems? Are we measuring our results rigorously enough? Another matter that I wish to address is human rights. Colombia defends human rights and will continue to do so. But my country believes that protecting human rights loses credibility when it becomes subjected to political calculation. I categorically reject human rights being used as a banner raised against some and lowered against others. Nor can human rights become an instrument rewarding friends, punishing adversaries, or worse still, remaining silent in line with the political circumstances of the time. Our duty is to prevent politics from weakening the defense of human rights. If we want the system to be respected, it needs to be serious, consistent and equally demanding on all of us. My country is consistent and therefore we want to ensure that we have a credible defense of human rights. And in this, just as in so many other areas, the United Nations still has some room for improvement. In that connection, we trust in a democratic transition in Venezuela, a swift, safe, far-reaching transition. There's another doctrinal concern that I wish to raise just as honestly, globalism. Allow me to begin by clarifying what I mean by that. I'm not talking about international trade or cooperation among states, nor am I talking about a humanity that shares common problems and responsibilities. All of those things are absolutely necessary. I'm talking about a concept according to which nation, sovereignty, distinct identities, traditions, and the values of peoples are obstacles that gradually give way to increasing political and cultural uniformity decided by supranational bodies. I don't share in that doctrine, which I consider perverse and harmful. For me, multilateralism isn't about dissolving nations, but rather about facilitating cooperation among them. Loving one's homeland isn't compatible with respecting others. Defending history, culture, values, and traditions doesn't mean disparaging those of another. International cooperation is richer when those who sit around this table know who they are, where they come from, and what the people in whose name they speak represent. Several of the questions that I've asked are not unfamiliar to this organization. The UN80 initiative has placed on the table issues of duplication, fragmentation, administrative burden, and the way mandates function as part of an effort to make the United Nations more efficient and more effective. President, Secretary-General, heads of state and government excellencies. Acknowledging an institution's imperfections doesn't mean overlooking its value. On the contrary, it might be a way of strengthening it. It has never been my style to hide behind political correctness or to tell my interlocutors what I imagine they want to hear. I'm not looking to please anyone, but rather to set out the position of the Republic of Colombia respectfully, cordially and clearly. No human institution is perfect. All can be improved, perfected, and the United Nations is no exception. There is one specific area that Colombia wishes to reflect on further, that is the international fight against terrorism. This organization has done significant work here. Since 1963, the international community has developed 19 universal legal instruments aimed at preventing different terrorist acts. However, after decades of discussion, there is still no legal definition of terrorism that is universally agreed by member states. The UN Office of Counterterrorism itself has recently flagged that the lack of a universally agreed definition begets legal uncertainty, discrepancies among national laws, and causes difficulties in international cooperation. The Republic of Colombia believes that the time has come to move ahead. Mr. President of the General Assembly, Heads of State and Government, Secretary-General, Ministers, distinguished delegates. President, on behalf of Senegal, I wish to thank your predecessor and convey to you my hearty congratulations.
