War in Ukraine, the Middle East, Sudan, Haiti, Yemen, and Africa, including the expansion of terrorism in the Sahel, all of these bear witness to the continued worsening and deep cracks in international peace and security. in Gaza and indeed throughout the OPT. Human suffering is unconscionable. There are systemic violations of international law and these are unacceptable. It is high time to act to halt the horror of mass murder and destruction. No country No peace, no security can be viable, nor can it last without the two-state solution, Palestine with East Jerusalem as its capital and Israel, the two living side by side within safe and internationally recognized borders. In a situation of ongoing conflict which favors an arms race, which erodes disarmament mechanisms and fuels risk linked to new technologies. And that the fact that there is an arms race in outer space in this context, we call for a collective stirring, peaking of our conscience. Peace is not a simple aspiration. It cannot be. Its stabilization must be pursued, it cannot be forgotten. Of course, there are worsening health crises. The Ebola epidemic is an example of just that. Global inequalities are increasing. The climate urgency has become an even more bitter reality. The human, economic, and social cost of these phenomenon continue to grow. There are many environmental perils facing our age. We need to act on all fronts. That is our ambition for the third United Nations Water Conference that Senegal will co-organize with the United Arab Emirates. It will be held this year. Ladies and gentlemen, a lasting peace cannot be decoupled from development. 40 years after the adoption of the Declaration on the Right to Development, we know what we need to do to achieve that goal. There also needs to be the implementation of the severe commitment as well as of the Pact for the Future. Senegal also believes in the transformative potential of new technologies, including the development of AI that is based on robust morals and ethical code based on the principle of responsibility and inclusion. The launch of our first satellite illustrates our desire to make space, AI and digital tools instruments that serve and foster human development. President, dear colleagues, we are all well aware of the challenges linked to the very life of our organization. Ours is a concerning financial situation. Indeed, these questions are being asked about peace operations, just as they are about the SDGs. The implementation of these is lagging behind, and significantly so. In view of this reality, It is true that some might be tempted to view multilateralism as a relic and might be tempted to move outside of multilateralism to take action in isolation. Senegal does not espouse that view. On the contrary, it is precisely because the world is beset by a whole host of unprecedented crises that we need a UN that is stronger, more representative and more effective. We will not settle crises by allowing the multilateral system to become ever more piecemeal. We will not achieve peace if we simply stage power struggles. We will not guarantee a just international order if we see right being replaced by might. Doing all of that will imperil the very raison d'etre of our organization, that is dialogue, conflict prevention, the peaceful resolution of disputes, cooperation and respect for international law. In this vein, and with this in mind, the UN80 initiative provides us with a historic opportunity to usher in the structural and normative transformations that we need to see. However, reforming the United Nations must not stymie its ambitions. On the contrary, it must make it less bureaucratic in how it functions. It must remove red tape, make it more agile, and make it more effective in its expenditure. And there must be better synergies between headquarters and the field so we can better serve the people we represent. Senegal supports that very dynamic. That was the rationale behind our contribution to efforts to strengthen the UN system. We've used our own resources to build a UN house some 30 kilometers away from Dakar. This is a cutting edge institution and the site will house all UN system entities in the region and that will foster greater coherence and effectiveness in the UN's work. However, a stronger organization and ensuring it is stronger also involves Member States upholding their financial pledges and making good on their assessed contributions. President, the years are ticking by, but our efforts to reform governance have yet to produce a significant impact. The status quo when it comes to reforming the Security Council bears witness to that fact. We all agree that the composition of the Security Council is out of step with the realities of our time. We agree that the expansion of the Council should not lead to further inertia. But given the fact the Council is lacking legitimacy, and that is indeed the hallmark of the Council's current structure, we cannot simply issue observations. We are in at a juncture where there is an urgent need for action. It's a matter of justice, credibility and balance across the international system. And this is indeed the rationale which underpins the Ezulwini Consensus, which outlines the African position in connection with the so necessary reform of the UN Security Council. However, beyond reform, the organization also needs experienced leadership. to steer its work in these times of crisis and uncertainty. In that Olympic spirit, I invite all Member States to attend the opening ceremony of the Youth Games on the 31st of October 2026 in Dakar, and I thank you for your kind attention.

The president of the United Nations General Assembly. the excellency Doctor Khalilur Rahman. The Secretary General, Mister Antonio Guterres. Fellow heads of state and government. Your excellencies, ladies and gentlemen. The assembly of Inaka. and a very good afternoon to you all. I bring warm greetings from the people of Fiji and from the blue Pacific continent. We face deepening geopolitical rivalry, armed conflict, and climate and environmental crisis, economic uncertainty, disrupted supply chains and rapid technological change, and an information environment corroded by disinformation. Mr. President, Fiji reaffirms an enduring principle. The international law is not optional. And peace cannot be secured by power alone. For small states, the principles of the charter, sovereign equality, territorial integrity, and the peaceful settlement of disputes are the safeguards against a world in which the size of military strength decides whose rights matters. When the world asks small states to choose between competing power blocks, Fiji chooses principles. And we choose the charter. We choose the international law. We choose dialogue over coercion, human dignity over domination, and cooperation over confrontation. Fiji calls for the peaceful settlement of conflicts wherever they occur. We urge all parties to protect civilians, respect international humanitarian law, and return to the negotiating table. The charter does not apply differently according to who is involved. OAU and Fiji ask the same of every party in every theater. Energy, food security, and supply chains are inseparable from peace. Dialogue is worth pursuing. And peace, however difficult, is always worth building. Mr. President, the Pacific knows the cost of militarization and nuclear testing. The Pacific welcomes our friendship, investment, and genuine cooperation. But our ocean must not become a theater in which others settle their rivalries. For small island developing states, regional cooperation is not an optional layer of diplomacy. It is a practical necessity separated by vast differences with small populations and narrow economic bases. And what is difficult alone becomes possible together. We must take it further still through connectivity, food and energy security, and Pacific-led financing, such as something the Pacific has built. The Pacific Resilience Facility is the first climate and disaster financing facility owned, governed, and hosted by the states it serves. Its treaty entered into force in May. And it is seated in the Kingdom of Tonga. And its first grants are already reaching our communities. It exists because a village seewall does not need a three-year aggregation process. All it needs is money that arrives or will arrive. Its essential capitalization target is $500 million United States dollar by December. of which 173 million has been pledged. I thank all those who have come forward, and I ask those who are able to close the gap to do so willingly. Cooperation of this kind does not diminish our sovereignty. It strengthens our ability to exercise it. And, Mr. President, the call to restore trust must also apply within our own nations. Fiji's democratic journey has not been easy. Together, they can carry Fiji from memory to understanding and from division to trust. Mr. President, if the United Nations is to restore trust, it must also be willing to reform itself. For Pacific small island developing states, efficiency must not mean distance. The multi-country offices serving our region are essential bridges between global commitments and island realities. Reform must strengthen and not thin our capacity to deliver where need is the greatest. This Assembly will also select the next Secretary-General. Fiji asks for a process that is transparent and merit-based, and for a Secretary-General who understands the realities of small island states, and more importantly, will act on them. For too long, our circumstances have been well diagnosed and poorly addressed. The promise to deliver for all must also be measured in development. With 2030 approaching, too many sustainable development goals remain off track. National income alone cannot capture remoteness, disaster exposure, and the repeated burden of rebuilding. The multidimensional vulnerability index must move from adoption to application. There is one measure of delivery that reaches Fijian households directly. Remittances are now Fiji's third largest source of foreign exchange. They pay for school fees, rebuild homes after lots of cyclones, and sustain families between harvests. Your Excellencies, they are not aid. They are the earnings of Fijians abroad and sent home. Yet, Pacific corridors remain among the most expensive in the world through which to send money. In May, in this august hall, we recommitted ourselves to bring transfer costs below 3% and to eliminate corridors costing more than 5%. Pacific corridors, among those Fiji asked, that is to be treated as an obligation and not an aspiration. Labour mobility must also not become a one-way transfer of the people that we have trained. Fiji does not regard any Fijian the chance to build a life abroad. We ask only that those who recruit our nurses and teachers invest in the systems that produce them. And this belongs beside what I have said of reconciliation. Not every Fijian abroad left in search of work. Some left in season of upheaval when they did not feel that the country was theirs. They are Fijians still and so are their children. A supreme law that belongs to every citizen must belong to them also. Fiji's door is open. This month, Fiji declared a national HIV emergency. Your Excellencies, One in 60 of our adults is now estimated to be living with the virus. Fewer than four in 10 know that. I say this plainly because stigma and silence are now how this epidemic grew. And because of the late Ratu Apeti Naile Takaue, our former head of state and UNAIDS Goodwill Ambassador for the Pacific, spent his last years telling us so. This is also a security question. Methamphetamine trafficked into our region by transnational criminal networks is now driving transmission through injecting drug use. Our borders are ocean. Our populations are small. And the profits at stake exceed our national budgets. A country such as Fiji of under a million people cannot interdict a global supply chain alone. So Fiji asked three things. That treatment and diagnostics reach small states at prices we can pay. And that the Global Fund and UNH be resourced at a level that does not force triage between regions. And that our partners treat Pacific narcotics interdiction as the shared security interest it is. These are the same laws. A nurse who emigrates is a nurse Fiji trained and will not have, because they've left. A Fijian who dies 35 of a treatable virus is the same subtraction, made permanent with the cost of care left behind. Small states are not losing workers at the margin. We are losing the capacity to staff our own future. Mr. President, nowhere is the deep gap between the promise and the delivery more consequential than in the climate crisis. For the Pacific, climate change is not a future scenario. It is saltwater entering farmland, coastal erosion moving closer to homes, and stronger storms damaging schools and roads. and the pressure on fisheries and food security and communities facing relocation. This is a question of science and it is also a question of justice, Your Honour. This Assembly has this week addressed the threats posed by sea level rise. Maritime zones once lawfully established and deposited within the United Nations, must remain, notwithstanding the physical changes brought by the sea level rise. Obligations recognized by the court must be reflected in national commitments, in the conduct of states, and in the outcomes of our negotiations. Climate finance must move from promise to access, from announcement to disbursement. The loss and damage fund must operate at a scale that reflects actual need. And access must be simplified. For small administration, the cost of applying should never exceed the capacity to apply. In November, the world gathers in Antalya for COP31. And before that, Fiji hosts the PRECOP and Tuvalu, a leaders event in early October. To every delegation in this august hall, come to the Pacific. See what a rising sea means to a village that has nowhere to move. Then let us go to Antalya and deliver on adaptation, on finance, and on loss and damage, and on the transition away from fossil fuels. As a large ocean state, Fiji's identity, economy and the future are inseparable from the ocean. Illegal fishing, pollution, biodiversity loss and warming and acidifying seas do not respect national boundaries. No island nation can meet them alone. This year, the Agreement on Marine Biodiversity Beyond National Jurisdiction entered into force. a genuine achievement of multilateralism, and Fiji calls for universal ratification for a first conference of the parties that delivers a functioning institution and for capacity building, technology transfer that are real rather than aspirational. And in the deep sea, we ask for others not only to discipline, not only the discipline, but we ask ourselves, no exploitation proceed until the science is sufficient and the rules are sound. The common heritage of humankind is an obligation owed to those not yet born. Mr. President, Fiji comes to this great assembly as a small island state, but not with a small vision. Our size does not diminish our voice. Our vulnerability does not diminish our agency. And our distance from the centers of power does not distance us from its consequences. Transformation will happen, whether we manage it or not, Your Excellencies. And the real question is, what kind of transformation we choose? Will it be governed by law or by power? And will this great assembly remain a place where we come to describe crisis or become an institution that solves it? Let this 81st session be remembered, and not for the depth of our concern, but for the courage of our decisions. Let us build a United Nations that is trusted because it is fair, relevant because it adapts, and respected because it delivers. Let us build a Pacific that remains an ocean of peace, united in purpose, confident in its identity, and strong enough to shape its own future. And let us remember that the measure of what we do here will not be found in our speeches. It will be found in whether a coastal community can remain on the land of its ancestors, and whether a young person can trust democracy and find future at their home. That is the United Nations Fiji believes in, and that is the trust we must restore together. And once again, vinaka vaka levu, and I thank you.

Mr. President of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly, Your Excellencies, Heads of State and Government, Mr. Secretary-General of the United Nations, ladies and gentlemen. On behalf of His Excellency Mr. Alassane Ouattara, President of the Republic of Cote d'Ivoire, and of the Government and people of Cote d'Ivoire, I wish to extend our warm congratulations to the President of the General Assembly on his election to preside over the 81st session of our organization and to assure him of Cote d'Ivoire's full support in the discharge of his important mandate. And as his tenure draws to a close, I would also like to pay a heartfelt tribute to the Secretary-General of the United Nations, Mr. Antonio Guterres. Over the past decade, he has exercised his high office with profound humanity and absolute fidelity to the ideals of the Charter of the United Nations in an international context that has been among the most trying in the contemporary history of our organization. wishes to express its deep gratitude to him for the excellence of our cooperation, which has grown stronger throughout his term. Mr. Secretary-General, President Alassane Ouattara has asked me to convey to you his warmest regards grounded in high esteem and friendship, as well as his sincere wishes for success in the next chapters of your distinguished career. Mr. President, Excellencies, Ladies and Gentlemen, This session is taking place against a deeply troubling international backdrop. Conflicts and hotspots of tension are multiplying and geopolitical divisions are deepening, while the rise of terrorism and violent extremism threatens an ever-growing number of regions. At the same time, climate upheavals are hitting our countries hard, not to mention the humanitarian crises and deep inequalities that are weakening our societies. Added to this are the very real risks to the survival of humanity posed by the uncontrolled development of artificial intelligence. The world is thus at a difficult turning point. It is looking on at the gradual fragmentation of its peace architecture and an alarming reconfiguration of the international landscape. Before our very eyes, multilateralism is being sorely tested, weakened by an erosion of trust between nations and trust in the institutions that underpin the world order. In these times of multilateral fracture, it is imperative to find appropriate solutions to put an end to these dangerous escalations, prioritize dialogue, and rebuild trust. With regard to international institutions, this trust is measured by their ability to translate the universality of their principles into concrete actions and to treat every state, large or small, with the same standard of fairness. The trust of peoples, for its part, is nourished by tangible results and by the certainty that the decisions taken on their behalf genuinely serve their security, their dignity, and protect their future. This year's theme therefore aptly captures the expectations of our time. It calls on us specifically to restore trust in our collective capacity to respond effectively to global challenges and to support the current changes and reforms of the United Nations architecture so that our organization is once again able to deliver concrete solutions to the concerns of all peoples. For Cote d'Ivoire, this means reinvigorating multilateralism and consequently restoring diplomacy's rightful place and credibility so that it can

effectively. In light of these challenges, a monumental task awaits the next Secretary-General of the United Nations, whose selection process is now well underway. Cote d'Ivoire hopes that this process will result in the appointment of a figure of the highest caliber, whose moral values, independence of mind, diplomatic experience, and commitment to dialogue will enable the United Nations to pursue with ambition and effectiveness its mission in the service of peace, development, and solidarity among nations. Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, current international events remind us every day of the human, political, and economic cost of protracted conflicts. Cote d'Ivoire remains deeply concerned about the resumption of hostilities in the Near and Middle East, the consequences of which weigh on peace and on food, energy, and economic security throughout the world. The dire situation in the East of the Democratic Republic of the Congo and in the Sudan is equally alarming with severe and endless humanitarian consequences. All these persistent conflicts are exacerbating the suffering of the affected populations and producing harmful effects that extend far beyond the borders of the states concerned. We therefore call for dialogue to prevail over arms. We also express our solidarity with the Haitian people. Cote d'Ivoire will continue to contribute to ongoing initiatives aimed at supporting the Haitian authorities and international partners in order to restore security in the sister nation so as to restore democratic legitimacy to its institutions. My country takes this opportunity to reaffirm its commitment to the peaceful settlement of disputes in accordance with the United Nations Charter. And to lend its full support for the many mediation efforts undertaken by the United Nations, the African Union, and relevant regional organizations. Ladies and gentlemen, Africa is bearing the brunt of the decline of multilateralism and the difficulties the United Nations has faced in recent years. Due to a lack of support from certain partners and from the United Nations, several African countries are struggling to find lasting solutions to conflicts and to bear the cost of various counterterrorism and peacekeeping operations. Meanwhile, violent extremism, transnational organized crime, and illicit trafficking of all kinds continue to destabilize a number of regions on the continent, and in particular, the Sahel. Our experience and the realities on the ground demonstrate that no state can, on its own, overcome such threats in a definitive and lasting manner. This requires greater regional cooperation and international solidarity in order to ensure appropriate responses. These threats also call for investment in conflict prevention and for addressing at an early stage the vulnerabilities that fuel crises, including poverty, inequality, youth unemployment, and all other forms of marginalization. In this regard, we commend the efforts of the United Nations, the African Union, ECOWAS, and all the partners working on security and stabilization efforts in our region. If these institutions are to be as effective as expected, they must therefore become more representative, more inclusive, and better attuned to the demands of our time. Indeed, it is becoming increasingly difficult to explain to younger generations that organizations created in the aftermath of the Second World War can no longer faithfully reflect the political, demographic, and economic realities of the 21st century. My country once again reaffirms its support for an ambitious reform of the Security Council so as to ensure permanent representation for Africa in this important body whose decisions directly affect our peace and security. That is why Cote d'Ivoire welcomes the progress achieved through the Pact for the Future and calls for its swift implementation. The real challenge is no longer to adopt new commitments, but rather to translate those already made into tangible results for the greater well-being of our peoples. Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, there can be no lasting peace without truly inclusive and equitable development. As the 2030 deadline approaches, progress towards achieving the sustainable development goals remains insufficient, while financing needs remain considerable in many developing countries. The fourth international conference on financing for development rightly recalled that the necessary resources exist. The challenge now lies in our collective ability to mobilize them and to channel them with greater equity, solidarity, and effectiveness in the service of sustainable development. Cote d'Ivoire therefore calls for an ambitious reform of the international financial architecture and a renewed global partnership. to ensure that developing countries have more equitable access to the resources needed to finance infrastructure, health, education, energy, industrial transformation, and the creation of decent jobs for young people. Climate challenges require a similar degree of mobilization. Africa contributes the least to global greenhouse gas emissions, yet remains among the regions most hit the hardest by their consequences. Droughts, floods, land degradation, and the disruption of food systems directly threaten the ways of life and the livelihoods of millions of people. In this context, honouring international commitments on climate finance, adaptation and technology transfer is an imperative of justice and solidarity. Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, the transformation that our world is experiencing is also a technological one. Artificial intelligence and the digital revolution are opening up considering opportunities in many areas of our contemporary world. However, these technological advances can also exacerbate existing divides if their development as well as access to them remain unevenly distributed. In this regard, Cote d'Ivoire supports the efforts of the United Nations to promote the global governance of artificial intelligence that fosters innovation while protecting human dignity, international security, and sustainable development in a spirit of inclusion, ethics, and equitable sharing of the benefits of technological progress. Mr. President, the trust that we seek at the international level must also be built within each of our states. through the strength of our institutions and our ability to create the conditions for sustainable and shared development. My country, for its part, under the leadership of President Alassane Ouattara, continues on its path towards a stronger and more diversified economy while taking care to ensure and safeguard peace and stability. This ambition is now embodied in Cote d'Ivoire's National Development Plan 2026-2030, which is part of a long-term vision aligned with the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and the African Union's Agenda 2063. Our ambition remains to build a prosperous and united nation where economic growth translates into greater opportunity, social progress and well-being for all of our people. Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, as the United Nations enters its ninth decade of existence, we have a collective duty to demonstrate that multilateralism remains the best response to the challenges of our time. We must choose dialogue over confrontation, cooperation over isolation, and solidarity over indifference. We must restore trust among nations, ensure that the rule of law prevails over the use of force, place human beings at the heart of our decisions, and make our diversity a source of strength rather than a cause for division. Only then will the United Nations continue to embody the hopes of peoples and fulfill the promises that led to its creation. Cote d'Ivoire, true to its values and firmly committed to peace, dialogue, and multilateralism, will continue with humility but with determination to contribute to this collective endeavor because we believe that the destiny of humanity remains profoundly shared. Finally, it is incumbent upon us to ensure that the United Nations remains for present and future generations a true crucible of human dignity and the guarantor of a better world. I thank you.

Nigeria demands, in accordance with the Delwin consensus and the safety declaration, at least two permanencies for Africa. With all the rights and responsibilities of permanent membership, including the veto, for as long as it exists, and five non-permanent seats in total. Her Majesties, Excellencies, Highnesses, distinguished delegates, Mr. President of the General Assembly, Mr. Secretary-General, ladies and gentlemen. 12 years could be in politics a mere temporal span, the length of a protracted crisis. But for a Yemeni child, 12 years are his entire childhood. An entire generation was born amid war, grew up amid hunger, fear, and weapons, learning the names of mines before learning the alphabet of life. We do not ask the world to mourn every Yemeni child whose future has been stolen. Rather, we ask how many more children must be deprived of their future before the world stands resolutely with the Yemeni people and their struggle to restore their state and their stability. The people of Yemen, Yemen, this great nation with its rich history, civilization, and human heritage, has been enduring for 12 years the consequences of the coup carried out by the terrorist Houthi militia against the state and its institutions. 12 years. 12 years marked by war, displacement, poverty, recruitment of children, terrorizing of women, laying of mines, confiscation of rights, freedoms, and public resources. Ladies and gentlemen, the government of Yemen has engaged responsibly and positively with all international and regional initiatives and has made significant concessions in pursuit of peace and an end to the suffering of the Yemeni people. However, the terrorist Houthi militias have responded to those efforts with intransigence, using periods of humanitarian truces to advance their military arsenals at the expense of the livelihoods of ordinary citizens. The latest of these efforts was the initiative undertaken by the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia and the Sultanate of Oman to elaborate a roadmap toward peace. The Yemeni government accepted that initiative, while the Houthi militias rejected it and instead escalated their actions in the Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb to serve an Iranian agenda that goes beyond the interests of Yemen and its people, turning one of the world's most important waterways into a tool of pressure and bargaining. in Iran's confrontation with the world. Ladies and gentlemen, this coup could not have persisted for so many years, nor could its threat have expanded from Yemen to neighboring states and international waterways without the military support expertise, and technology provided to the Houthi militias by the rogue Iranian regime. The international community's hesitation to designate the Houthis as a terrorist group provided them with a valuable opportunity to expand their influence and magnify the threat they pose. We have seen that decisive action, when applied, weakens their capabilities. The coalition to restore legitimacy in Yemen led by the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia has played a critical role in reducing the dangers posed by this group through its support for the Yemeni government, thereby contributing to regional and international security and stability. We believe that this firm approach adopted by the United States administration in dealing with the Houthi militias has disrupted their calculations. The Yemeni government appreciate President Trump's clear understanding of the only language this terrorist group comprehends, the language of resolve. It is the language that leaves no room for misinterpretation. We likewise value the support of every friendly state that has stood behind this position. International legitimacy and its resolutions are there, but resolutions alone do not make peace. An international resolution without a political will to implement it does not stop wars. Rather, it merely prolongs a marathon of negotiations while only terrorism advances. Peace is not a distant aspiration. It is a firm determination. It is an effective deterrent action against those who threaten the security and stability of states. Ladies and gentlemen, Iranian support is not the only factor contributing to the danger posed by Houthi terrorist militias. They also benefit from the lack of an effective and decisive international position. They benefit from every statement that underestimates the threat represented by this racist terrorist movement in Yemen. In Yemen, We're not confronting a purely local terrorist militia. Rather, we face an extension of the Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps, which is also using terrorist groups to threaten international peace and security. The Houthi militias use of the safety of navigation as a tool for blackmail threaten not only Yemen. taking hostage the entire global economy. Recent years have clearly demonstrated a truth that the international community must not dismiss, namely that ensuring security at sea begins with eliminating the source of the threat on land. Protecting ships is important, but it only addresses the consequences and does not remove the threat. Therefore, we warn the world. Do not be reassured by false promises from a terrorist militia that has repeatedly made endless commitments just as it failed to honor them. Its abstention from targeting ships today does not mean at all it will not do so tomorrow. It is a strategic mistake. It is a strategic mistake to assume that maritime security can be sustained through assurances that can be walked back. A lasting maritime security in the Red Sea, Bab el-Mandeb, and the Gulf of Aden cannot be built while a non-state armed militia remains on the shores. Nor is the threat confined to Yemen and the Red Sea. international reports have exposed growing cooperation between the terrorist Houthi militias and terrorist organizations, including in the Horn of Africa, through networks linking militias, terrorist groups, smugglers, and organized crime networks, thereby undermining states and threatening security and stability. Ladies and gentlemen, we say with full confidence and we firmly believe that restoring the Yemeni state and restoring the security of Bab el-Mandeb are inseparable. They are not two separate issues, but one and the same. Supporting the Yemeni government and strengthening its economic security and military capacities is an investment in international peace and security. Protecting this strategic waterway is a shared regional and international responsibility which Yemen cannot shoulder alone. It is the responsibility of every economy that depends on secure supply chains, energy security, and freedom of navigation. In this regard, we commend the initiative of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia to establish a multinational maritime defense coalition. This initiative reflects a deep appreciation and understanding of collective responsibility to protect navigation, deter threats, and combat smuggling. The path to a secure at sea requires a stable Yemen. There is no stability in Yemen without restoring the state. Sustainable peace cannot be achieved while an armed militia remains above the law and outside state authority. Restoring the Yemeni state is not just a national interest, it is a direct contribution to regional security and stability, and to the protection of one of the world's most vital maritime corridors. Ladies and gentlemen, our Yemeni people aspires to peace, but our people will not abandon their state. Our government is committed to peace, but it cannot accept that the armed coup becomes a fait accompli. There is no peace with arms outside state authority. Peace requires deeds, not words. 12 years of an incomplete peace have left millions of people enduring hunger, injuries, displacement. Every statistic in Yemen's tragedy carries a human story. The world must not become accustomed to the suffering. Yemen is a great country with its strategic location, its ports, its resources, its human capital. The challenge lies in unleashing those capabilities from the grip of war and transforming these capabilities into an engine for development today. The heroes of the Yemeni armed forces and all military formations, legitimate military formations, are on the ground confronting these Houthi terrorist militias in defense of our people, our land, our sovereignty, and our future. Here from this very podium, I salute them. I salute their struggle. They stand today to prevent much greater harm from reaching this world. We tell them from here, You are our people. Your suffering is our suffering. Your rights are our responsibility. You will never be outside the national project of a Yemeni state, nor outside its future. Our struggle is not against any Yemeni citizen, nor against the sons of any region, governorate, any sect or social group. Our struggle is against an armed coup that has taken hostage the state and its institutions, that deepened the suffering of Yemen and Yemenis to serve Iran and its schemes. Restoring the state is not a victory for one Yemeni party over another. It is the restoration of the rights of all Yemenis to their state and institutions. The Yemen for which we struggle belongs to all Yemenis. The state we seek to restore is your state. The future of Yemen will not be built by excluding any of its sons. Our cause is not merely about how to end the war, but to build what comes after it. We seek a safe, stable, prosperous Yemen that safeguards the dignity of its citizens, rebuilds its economy, provides education for its children, jobs for its youth, security for its families. Yemen that's a partner for its neighbors, a responsible guardian of its strategic location, a bridge for trade and cooperation between the Arabian Peninsula, the Horn of Africa, and the wider world. That is the Yemen that we wish for the world to see. Not a Yemen of war, but a Yemen of statehood, of humanity, of opportunity, a Yemen of the future, ladies and gentlemen. The Yemeni people do not ask the world to fight their battle on their behalf. They are determined to restore their state, rebuild its institutions, and confront terrorism in all its forms. What we ask? is that the international community fulfill its responsibilities, implement its resolutions, stop the flow of arms and technologies to the militias, support our national capacities and economy. The Yemeni government is capable of ending the threat posed by the terrorist group and protecting Yemen's ports and territorial waters. What we seek from the international community today is not a perpetual management of crises, but a strategic partnership that promotes security, stability, and development for the benefit of Yemen, the region, and international peace and security. We do not ask the world to build Yemen's future for Yemenis. We seek a partnership that supports the state and its institutions and invests in Yemen's people. For our part, we will continue to fulfill our responsibilities and reform institution building and the rule of law. The international community can find in the Yemeni government a reliable partner. We speak not only of what Yemen needs from the world, but also of what Yemen can contribute to the world once it regains its security and its stability. Ladies and gentlemen, we express our deep appreciation to the brotherly Kingdom of Saudi Arabia for its unwavering support for Yemen, its people, and its government, and for the Kingdom's comprehensive support to the state and its institutions. The Kingdom has borne and continues to bear significant burdens in support of Yemen's security and stability. These efforts will remain firmly engraved in the memory of the Yemeni people. From this podium, the Republic of Yemen condemns the terrorist attacks carried out by the Houthi militias against the Kingdom, targeting its territory, facilities, and resources. We equally condemn their attempted targeting of Mecca al-Mukarrama, to which the hearts and prayers of Muslims turn. We stand in solidarity with the kingdom and reaffirm Yemen's steadfast support for the kingdom's right to defend its territory, its citizens, and its national interests. Ladies and gentlemen, the Republic of Yemen, reaffirms its unwavering support for the Palestinian people's right to freedom, dignity, and the establishment of their independent sovereign state in accordance with international resolutions and the Arab Peace Initiative. We equally express our appreciation to the United Nations, the Secretary-General and his Special Envoy, as well as all UN agencies for their efforts in support of peace and in assistance to the Yemeni people. And we value the support of friends and partners standing by the Yemeni people. At the same time, We condemn the continued detention by the Houthi militias of UN personnel and humanitarian workers. Those working for peace and humanitarian relief must never be held hostage or blackmailed. I wish all the peoples of the world prosperity, peace, and development. and we hope for a world that is more secure, just, stable, and prosperous. And in conclusion, I extend my congratulations to our great Yemeni people at home and abroad on the occasion today, on the occasion of the 60th anniversary of the revolution of the 26th of September. We reaffirm our commitment to the values and objectives of the September and October revolutions and to the principles of our national struggle, principles that are non-negotiable with determination of the Yemenis, their sacrifices and perseverance, Yemen will regain its security and its stability. Bab al-Mandab will remain as geography intended it to be, a bridge between peoples, a route for commerce, and a gateway to peace. Allow me to conclude this statement with words by a Yemeni poet expressing faith in the Yemeni people, Yemeni homeland and future, and affirming that Yemen belongs to its free people, not to Iran, nor to its proxies. He said, "We are the land, its custodians and its inhabitants. To us it belongs. for we are its people and its home. Today belongs to the people. And yesterday, the glorious yesterday, belongs to them as well. To them belong the future, history, and time itself. Long live Yemen, free, secure, and great. May the peace and blessings be upon you all.

On behalf of the Assembly, I wish to thank the Prime Minister of the Republic of Armenia. The Assembly will now hear an address by His Excellency Anutin Charoen Virakul, Prime Minister of the Kingdom of Thailand. I request protocol to escort His Excellency. and invite him to address the Assembly.

Mr. President, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, at the outset, I congratulate you, Mr. President, on assuming the presidency of the 81st session of the General Assembly. It is an honor to address this assembly for the first time as being the Prime Minister of Thailand and as we mark 80 years of membership to the United Nations. When Thailand joined this organization, the post-war international order was still taking shape. Today, it is being reshaped once again. many of its old certainties are giving way. But what comes next is not yet settled. We are seeing many transformations taking place. Power is becoming more fragmented. Strategic competition is becoming sharper. And international rules are under strain. At the same time, technology is transforming our societies, while climate change is testing our resilience. Our institutions, however, are struggling to keep pace. Confidence in our ability to work together is weakening. And that is why this year's theme speaks directly to the task before us. Managing the transformation requires trust, trust between countries, Trust in the rules we share and trust that our institutions can deliver. But trust cannot be taken for granted. It must be earned. Trust weakens when principles are applied selectively, when countries have little say in decisions that shape their future, and when promises made in this Assembly fail to improve lives beyond it. Rebuilding trust means addressing each of these concerns. We must uphold common principles consistently. We must give countries a genuine stake in the international system, including a stronger voice for the global South. And we must take shared responsibility for turning commitments into results. Mr. President, the UN's purposes remain as relevant as ever to promote peace and security, human rights and dignity, sustainable development, and cooperation among sovereign equals. But we cannot build lasting peace if security is assured for some and denied to others. Universal human rights lose their meaning when applied selectively. Development loses its purpose when prosperity remains in the hands of a few. For Thailand, peace means more than the absence of war. It requires dialogue to settle differences and respect for international law so that all countries can live with security and dignity. The situation in Palestine continues to demand our attention. It reminds us that the principles we uphold must protect people when they need them the most. That is why human rights must be universal in practice. As a member of Human Rights Council, Thailand believes that our work must reach beyond resolutions and make a real difference in people's lives. Development must be people-centered and sustainable. Growth must improve people's lives today without closing off the opportunities of tomorrow. Consistent application of principles gives countries the confidence that they will be treated fairly But that confidence must also extend to how decisions are made. Countries need to know that their voices count. Mr. President, the UN's membership has become nearly universal, but representation has not evolved at the same pace. An international system cannot command trust if large parts of its membership feel they have too little to say in shaping it. Rebuilding trust requires shared ownership. The United Nations must reflect today's world, not the distribution of power 80 years ago. And that is why Thailand supports Security Council reform that gives developing countries and underrepresented regions, particularly in the global south, a greater role in decision making. Asia, too, must be better represented for all its economic weight. Asia must be able to help shape global decisions and carry more responsibility for the outcomes. And representation must also mean that women have a meaningful voice in the decisions that shape our common future. They are already at the forefront of this organization's work from development to peacekeeping. As the UN considers its next Secretary General, maybe it is time that this representation be reflected at the highest level. Representation and effectiveness must advance together. We commend Mr. Secretary General Antonio Guterres for his commitment to reform, including through the UN80 initiative. We stand ready to work with his successor to carry this work forward. Mr. President, having a stronger voice in global institutions means countries working together on the problems closest to them. This is where regional cooperation has a vital role. The United Nations must remain the centerpiece of the multilateral system, but we cannot expect it to do everything. It cannot settle problems when member states are not willing to act. Regional institutions can help turn that willingness into cooperation. They bring countries together around share challenges and translate global principles suited to local realities. In this way, regionalism becomes a building block of effective multilateralism. ASEAN has demonstrated this for almost six decades. It has grown from five to 11 member states. We do not always agree. but we have learned to manage differences and preserve space for cooperation. For my country, Thailand, that practical cooperation means serving as a trusted platform. We want to leverage our strengths as a logistical hub and manufacturing base to connect markets and supply chains across our region. Our conviction is that together we should combine Asia's diversity for co-creation, bringing together the different strengths of our countries to promote shared prosperity. The same thinking should also extend beyond Asia. Thailand continues to pursue free trade agreements with partners across region. and to expand trade and opportunities for both sides. Additionally, our Thailand Africa initiative seeks to deepen political, economic and development cooperation to build partnerships of equals across our regions. Mr. President, Excellencies, distinguished delegates. Institution earn trust through what their members are prepared to do. A greater voice must come with a willingness to contribute. Shared ownership, therefore, must lead to shared responsibility. The charter begins with the words, "We, the peoples." Thailand believes that this work must begin at home. The SDG Sustainable Development Goals provide us with an important framework that goes beyond development. Ultimately, they are about enabling people to live in peace and dignity. Progress towards achieving the SDGs also shapes how we are building a strong and resilient economy and how we remain accountable to our people. Thailand will leverage our strengths. We are building upon our strong agricultural base to be a source of food security for the world. Meanwhile, our universal health coverage ensures that people have access to affordable and quality health care, while also developing Thailand into a medical and wellness hub. Additionally, Our energy transition efforts take Thailand closer to meeting climate obligations. And through our solar rooftop policy, we are also creating greater economic opportunities for households by allowing them to sell excess electricity back to the grid. However, this responsibility goes beyond development. Thailand's humanitarian tradition demonstrates this conviction. In the late '70s, we provided temporary refuge and assistance to large numbers of Cambodians fleeing violence and famine. Today, we are giving displaced persons from Myanmar, who have lived in temporary shelters in Thailand for decades, greater opportunities to work and support their families. For the Rohingya transiting in Thailand, we have adopted a community-based alternative to immigration detention for Rohingya children to better protect their rights and access to services. Our responsibility as a neighbor also means addressing the challenges in our own neighborhood. One of those challenges is the dispute between our country and our neighbor, being Cambodia. We have been through a difficult period. When I met with Prime Minister Hun Manet in May, we sought to resolve difficult issues through bilateral dialogue, where rebuilding trust and confidence in order to move forward together. It is regrettable that Cambodia did not give dialogue a genuine chance and chose a different path by initiating compulsory conciliation proceedings under UNCLOS. Nevertheless, Thailand is engaging in good faith, but our position is clear. This process concerns the delimitation of maritime boundaries only. In the meantime, Cambodia must work with us to strengthen security along our shared border, including through concrete cooperation to combat online scams and demining. Our communities will not be safe if we do not make concrete progress on these matters. Ultimately, Our shared border must be a place of shared prosperity, not one that continues to bear the scars of conflict. Let me be clear, Thailand has never sought conflict, but peace can only be built when we work together in earnest. And surely this will require genuine effort from our neighbor, Cambodia. That same commitment guides our approach to Myanmar. Thailand supports peace, national reconciliation, and a durable solution that is Myanmar-led and Myanmar-owned. We believe in constructive and calibrated re-engagement within ASEAN and in coordination with relevant partners while encouraging concrete progress on the ground. In both cases, our responsibility is to make dialogue possible and progress achievable. And when threats cross borders, responsibility must be shared more widely. My country has stepped up efforts on prevention and suppression of narcotics through our partnership with the UNODC. other regional and international organizations, as well as neighboring countries. And through the Global Partnership Against Online Scams, Thailand is bringing all the relevant stakeholders together to prevent these crimes. Mr. President, 80 years ago, in our first address to this Assembly, The Kingdom of Siam affirmed that it followed the path of peaceful settlement and friendly cooperation. That path still guides Thailand today. As a new international order takes shape, we must carry that spirit forward. No country can write its future alone, and no international order can earn lasting trust if too many countries feel that the system is written for them but not with them. A rule-based international order with shared ownership in shaping our common future is the condition that will help rebuild that trust. The future of United Nations will depend on the trust we rebuild through our action today. Let us give every nation reason to believe in the United Nations and every person reason to believe that the United Nations can deliver for them. Thank you very much.

Mr. President, Mr. Secretary-General, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, dear friends of Georgia. It's a privilege to stand before this Assembly on behalf of Georgia, a nation shaped by centuries of history, resilience, and engagement with a changing world. We meet at a time of considerable change in the international environment. Developments in different parts of the world are challenging existing arrangements and raising questions about the future of the international order. In this context, maintaining peace and strengthening international cooperation remain key priorities. In light of the growing number of global challenges, coordinated responses to common obstacles, conflict prevention, and the achievement of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development are possible only through strengthened international cooperation and their shared commitment to collective action. Lasting peace cannot be imposed by force, it must be built through communication, and mutual respect. Few countries understand the value of peace, stability, and sovereignty as deeply as Georgia does. For centuries, we stood at the crossroads of civilizations, open to diverse cultures, peoples, and ideas, while steadfastly preserving our own distinct identity and character. Georgia's statehood has been tested more than once, but these challenges have only strengthened our determination to choose our own path. The trials of history have also taught us that sovereignty can never be taken for granted, that stability must be protected, and the strength of the international order ultimately depends on the same principles being upheld for every nation. Our commitment to these principles carries particular meaning for Georgia. Twenty percent of our country remains under the occupation of the Russian Federation, while hundreds of thousands of our citizens continue to live in displacement, unable to return to their homes. While restoring trust is a major theme of this year's session, I would like to address our Abkhaz and Ossetian brothers and sisters. We have shared a homeland and a history for centuries. The divisions of today cannot erase that history, nor should they determine the future of our children. We believe that the dividends of peace and economic growth of Georgia should know no artificial boundaries. It must reach the people living in our occupied historic regions as well, who remain and will always remain part of our shared future. The challenges facing our country also remind us that national stability and success cannot be separated from the wider regional context. We believe that the South Caucasus should not be defined by the divisions of the past. We have consistently sought to act as an honest broker in regional initiatives, fostering cooperation and contributing to peaceful solutions. Today, we see a genuine opportunity to turn a new page and build a more peaceful and interconnected region based on shared commitment to a better future. This period of cooperation must also translate into tangible economic opportunities for the region. As an integral part of the South Caucasus and the Middle Corridor, Georgia is well-positioned to strengthen connectivity between Central Asia and Europe. Our strategic location and direct access to the Black Sea facilitate trade and investment, linking landlocked countries in our wider region to global supply chains. Our network of free trade agreements provides access to a market of approximately 2.3 billion consumers. To support and further advance connectivity agenda, Georgia plans to invest USD 7 billion by 2032 in major transport infrastructure. modernizing the railway, developing the Anaklia deep seaport, building a new international airport in Tbilisi, and expanding the highway network. At the same time, we believe that physical and digital connectivity are two parts of the same strategic agenda. Through a Black Sea submarine fiber optic connection and next generation data infrastructure, Georgia aims to strengthen secure, resilient, and diversified digital links between Europe and Asia. These ambitions are underpinned by Georgia's strong economic performance. Over the past five years, our economy has grown by an average of 9.3% annually, and this momentum has continued in 2026, with growth reaching 7.9% in the first seven months of the year. As the International Monetary Fund projects, Georgia will deliver one of the fastest growth rates in the medium term among regional and European countries, averaging 5.4%. With one of the fastest growing economies worldwide, we are actively building an innovation-oriented, business-friendly environment that supports both local and foreign enterprises. Despite the global uncertainty, Georgia's FDI to GDP ratio is one of the highest among peer countries and averaged over 6% of GDP in 2021-2025, highlighting the confidence of investors in the country's growth potential. Georgia's FTI outlook is supported by a pipeline of large multi-year investment projects across transport and logistics, energy infrastructure, tourism, and real estate. Yet the true measure of success is how it improves people's lives. Strong economic performance must translate into tangible social outcomes, higher output per person, rising real wages, declining poverty, better employment opportunities, and greater economic resilience. We are already seeing these outcomes reflected in measurable improvements, including a triple decline in Georgia's poverty rate, which dropped from 21.3% to 7.1% since 2020. Yet this achievement is only part of the broader transformation we seek to achieve. Over the next five years, our focus will therefore be on narrowing disparities between urban and rural communities, expanding opportunities across every region, and ensuring that the benefits of economic growth are shared widely and that no one is left behind. These priorities are fully aligned with Georgia's commitment to the Sustainable Development Goals and are reflected in our new United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework for 2026-2030. Looking further ahead, our ambition for the coming decade is to transform Georgia from an upper-middle-income country into a high-income economy underpinned by greater economic diversification, a growing share of knowledge-based activities, and broad-based prosperity. Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, the progress we seek at home is inseparable from the cooperation we build beyond our borders. Georgia remains open to meaningful engagement with every international partner prepared to engage with us on the basis of mutual respect and sovereign equality. We believe that lasting partnerships are built through dialogue and never through pressure or coercion. The principles of respect and cooperation are also at the heart of effective multilateralism. At a time of growing global uncertainty, the United Nations remains indispensable as a forum for dialogue and collective action. In this regard, the UN80 initiative provides a valuable opportunity to strengthen the effectiveness and capacity of the United Nations, while further enhancing its transparency and accountability. Georgia stands ready to work constructively with international partners and contribute actively to this process. We firmly support reforms that will strengthen the organization's capacity to deliver better and become more results-oriented. The choice we make today will shape the world we leave to future generations. Let's ensure that we leave them a world that is more peaceful, secure, and united than the one we know today. Thank you very much.

On behalf of the Assembly, I wish to thank the Prime Minister of Georgia. The Assembly will hear an address by His Excellency, Tarik Rahman, Prime Minister of the Government of People's Republic of Bangladesh. I request protocol to escort His Excellency Tariq Raman and invite him to address the assembly.

Bismillahirrahmanirrahim. Mr. President, I congratulate you on your election as President of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly. I assure you of our full support and cooperation as you discharge your responsibilities as President. At the same time, I extend my gratitude to the outgoing President, Madam Annalena Baerbock, for her able leadership. Let me begin by paying my deepest respect to all the martyred freedom fighters of Bangladesh. I respectfully remember the contributions of those who have made the ultimate sacrifice in the struggle to establish democracy, justice and people's rights in our country since independence. I also pay my sincere respect to all those who were martyred and injured in the mass uprising of courageous students and people in July-August 2024 against fascism. After more than a decade, and a half of movement and struggle against fascist rule and exploitation, and through the sacrifice of thousands of lives, Bangladesh is now free from fascism. In a free, fair and impartial national election held on 12 February this year, the people entrusted the Bangladesh Nationalist Party with the responsibility of governing the country. I congratulate the democracy-loving people of Bangladesh We believe that the people are the source of all our political power. Standing on this world stage of the United Nations, I am somewhat nostalgic at this moment. It was from this very world stage that my father, Shaheed President Ziaur Rahman, the proclaimer of Bangladesh's independence, and my mother, former Prime Minister Late Begum Khaled Zia, addressed the world on behalf of the country and its people. Today, I too stand here to speak for the interests of my country and its people and in the hope of a peaceful world community. In this age of globalization, Whatever happens in any part of the world has, to varying degrees, a negative impact on every country. Human-made conflicts have created situations of unrest in many countries. Vast numbers of people are being displaced, giving rise to humanitarian crises. Wars and conflicts are placing immense pressure on the global economy. Energy security concerns, disruptions to global energy supply systems, and rising inflation are worsening the economic situation. We believe that every conflict should be resolved through dialogue, diplomatic processes, and mutual cooperation. Equality, fairness, protection of mutual interests, and respect and dignity among disputing states should form the basis of bilateral and multilateral relations. We aspire to a peaceful world, a humane global community, where rather than weapons of destruction, reason and debate, diplomacy, education and humanity become the instruments of change. Bangladesh sees the United Nations as the centerpiece for establishing an accommodative global community based on mutual respect for one another's independence and sovereignty. The tendency to divert development budgets towards military expenditure in different parts of the world reverses the direction of our journey towards global peace. As a peace-loving nation, Bangladesh remains committed to the goals of complete and general disarmament, preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons and arms control. I reiterate Bangladesh's support for any initiative at the United Nations dedicated to establishing world peace and serving humanity. The people of Bangladesh, who believe in democracy, remain deeply concerned about the plight of the freedom-seeking Palestinian people. Bangladesh once again reaffirms its unwavering support for their legitimate demands, including their right to self-determination and their right to establish an independent State of Palestine, Mr. President, In the prevailing global circumstances, the theme of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly, "Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation: A United Nations that Delivers for All," is highly relevant and timely. Bangladesh remains steadfast in its commitment to multilateralism in maintaining international peace and security. As Vice-Chair of the Peacebuilding Commission, Bangladesh continues to serve as a strong voice for sustainable peace, conflict prevention and inclusive peace. As a consistent contributor to United Nations peacekeeping missions, Bangladeshi peacekeepers are serving humanity in different parts of the world. The courageous participation of Bangladeshi women in peacekeeping missions, even under adverse circumstances, reflects our strong commitment to advancing the agenda of women, peace and security. This year, Bangladesh is observing the 40th anniversary of the Declaration on the Right to Development and the 25th anniversary of the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action. Migration is as old as human civilization. In many countries around the world, migrants make important contributions to the economies of both their countries of origin and their countries of destination. The government of Bangladesh is committed to ensuring regular, safe, and orderly migration. Bangladesh expects stronger global cooperation to ensure the rights, dignity, and well-being of migrants. Mr. President, for more than nine years, Bangladesh has been sheltering more than 1.2 million forcibly displaced Rohingya from Myanmar. This has placed immense pressure on our resources, environment, security and local communities. As a densely populated country, Bangladesh believes that the source and origin of the Rohingya crisis lie in Myanmar. Therefore, its solution also lies there. The only solution to this problem is the early, safe return of the displaced Rohingya people to their homeland, Myanmar. For a lasting solution to this crisis, Bangladesh expects firm and effective support from the United Nations and the international community. At the same time, I call upon the United Nations and the international community to continue life-saving assistance programs for the displaced Rohingya people until they can be repatriated to their own country, Myanmar. If the international community fails to ensure justice for the displaced Rohingya people, this could turn into a humanitarian crisis in the near future. Mr. President, Bangladesh is one of the countries most vulnerable to the adverse impacts of climate change. Although Bangladesh has contributed little to global carbon emissions, it is bearing the adverse consequences of climate change. In these circumstances, Bangladesh has chosen the path of building resilience and developing the capacity to survive and adapt. Therefore, Bangladesh expects stronger global cooperation at COP31 on climate justice, climate finance and adaptation support. The government of Bangladesh has strengthened its programs for environmental protection. As part of these efforts, the government has launched a program to plant 250 million trees across the country over the next five years. Emphasis has been placed on the use of clean energy and solar energy. With the aim of freeing the country from the scourge of floods and droughts, The government has also launched a program to excavate 20,000 kilometers of canal across the country. The government has also began work on the Teesta Master Plan and the Padma Barrage Project to increase freshwater flows into the world's largest mangrove forest, the Sundarbans, and to conserve water through large reservoirs. At the same time, while strengthening domestic measures for water conservation and pollution prevention, the Government has reaffirmed its commitment to cooperation on transboundary water management by signing the 1992 Water Convention. Mr. President, After ending more than a decade and a half of fascist rule and exploitation, Bangladesh became free from fascism in 2024. Having been freed from the scourges of enforced disappearances, killings, abductions, corruption, plunder, and money laundering that had become the norm under fascist rule, Bangladesh is now once again embarking on the path of democracy. To repair a Bangladesh battered by fascist rule and exploitation, the government is pursuing a three R strategy-- recovery, restoration, and reconstruction. A vast horizon of opportunities has now opened before Bangladesh. Taking advantage of the demographic dividend, the government has begun implementing extensive programs to transform the country's working age population into a skilled human resource. The government has also undertaken some forward-looking initiatives to create large-scale employment opportunities and transform Bangladesh into a manufacturing hub. In this endeavor, Bangladesh wants its development partners by its side. To create opportunities for young entrepreneurs, researchers, and innovators in the country to pursue start-up initiatives, the government has allocated US$50 million in the current fiscal year. Mr. President, More than half of the country's population is female. Therefore, women are at the forefront of all government plans for socio-economic transformation. The government is giving priority to women's education, women's employment, and the creation of women entrepreneurs. To promote women entrepreneurship, particularly in the small and medium-sized industrial sector, the government has expanded opportunities for cash financing for women. Free education opportunities up to the undergraduate level have been opened to women. The government seeks to ensure not only electoral democracy but also democratization of the economy so that the benefits of economic growth and prosperity reach every family and every citizen. To achieve this goal, the government has already launched assistance programs for economically disadvantaged people through various social protection programs, including the Family Card, Farmers Card, Sports Card, and e-Health Card. The government considers the Family Card, issued in the name of the female head of each household, a symbol of women's economic empowerment. It is also in the government's plans to introduce a universal card by integrating the various card introduced to provide support in different sectors. Mr. President, the government is implementing the 31 point program presented to the people before the national election of 12 February 2026. At least 73% of the activities under the government's 31-point program have a direct alignment and 27% an indirect alignment with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals and their guiding principle of "leave no one behind." The government hopes that through the implementation of these programs, development disparities between urban and rural areas will be reduced, while accountability and inclusive, sustainable development will be advanced across all areas of the 2030 Agenda. The Government of Bangladesh has accorded special importance to education, health and sports. The highest budgetary allocations in the country's history have been made in the education sector. Our plan is to increase budgetary allocation to education to 5% of GDP within next 5 years. A curriculum has been developed with emphasis on technical and practical education to ensure an employment oriented education system with strong ethical values. From the first grade, Primary school students are being provided with school bags and clothing, i.e. school uniforms, as well as free lunch. The government hopes that this will increase school enrollment and improve the quality of education. To establish sports as a profession, sports has been included as a subject in the education curriculum for the first time. As part of this initiative, more than 2 million students participated in a month-long nationwide football tournament for school students held last June. Mr. President, Science and technology will shape the future of the world. We are entering a new era of artificial intelligence, biotechnology and science. Technology is advancing very rapidly. but its opportunities are still not equally accessible to all. Bangladesh's large young population and growing digital capabilities have created new possibilities for us. To harness these opportunities, access to advanced technology, knowledge, and research must be brought within everyone's reach. We do not want today's digital divide to become tomorrow's artificial intelligence divide. Bangladesh respects innovation and intellectual property. At the same time, it is essential to ensure technology transfer, skills development, and affordable access to modern technologies for developing countries. No country should be left behind in this scientific advancement. Bangladesh stands ready to work together to build a fair and prosperous future for all. It is now time for the United Nations to adopt an effective policy framework so that the benefits of the development and rapid expansion of artificial intelligence and social media can be harnessed positively across countries. Mr. President, Bangladesh is awaiting graduation from the list of least developed countries. For Bangladesh, as well as for all other countries undergoing this process, sustained support in areas such as assured financing, greater market access, technology transfer, and capacity building is essential to make the graduation process sustainable. In the present world order, all countries are interdependent. Bangladesh believes that, particularly at the regional level, We can help one another achieve prosperity through the facilitation and expansion of trade, effective connectivity, and meaningful cooperation. The COVID-19 pandemic claimed the lives of millions of people around the world. But it also sent a message to the world: for the global community to survive, mutual assistance, empathy, and cooperation are indispensable. It is essential to ensure sustainable production of vaccines, therapeutics and diagnostic equipment in developing countries so that these are readily accessible to all. Mr. President, A state can never become strong by keeping its citizens powerless. Through ensuring the political and economic empowerment of the people, We want to build a prosperous, self-reliant, welfare-oriented, democratic state where everyone, irrespective of political affiliation, religion or ethnicity, can live with security and peace and with equal rights, honor and dignity. Mr. President, Bangladesh continues to make progress in all areas. including democracy, human rights, good governance, accountability, political stability, and the investment environment. The government is working to establish a safe and stable Bangladesh with a business and investment friendly environment. In today's democratic Bangladesh, we welcome partnership, innovation, and both domestic and foreign investment. We want to build a Bangladesh where young people can pursue their dreams without fear or hindrance, where women can lead their lives with confidence, where every child grows up with the opportunity to realize their full potential, and, above all, where people are assured of a safe and peaceful life. That is why we say Bangladesh first, Bangladesh for all. I conclude my address by reaffirming Bangladesh's unwavering commitment to the values and principles of the United Nations in order to build a peaceful world. Mr. President, thank you. Alafiz Bangladesh Zindabad.

On behalf of the assembly, I wish to thank Mr. Tarik Rahman, Prime Minister of the People's Republic of Bangladesh. Thank you. I request protocol to escort his Excellency and invite him to address the Assembly.

Mr. President, your Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, Anne Frank was a teenage girl without power or influence, which had a pen and a diary, a diary that would make its way into the world and inspire millions of people. And I think that one of the reasons people are so inspired by Anne is that she had an unshakable belief in the power of people to turn the tides so that good prevails. She wrote, and I quote, "How wonderful it is that nobody needs to wait a single moment before starting to improve the world." And these words are just as powerful and true today. This week is the perfect example of that. And I realize that the United Nations does not carry the most positive associations for everyone. And indeed, there is much that can and must be improved. But let us not forget what lay behind the founding of the United Nations over 80 years ago, the realization that doing nothing had led to the darkest chapters in human history. And we now live in a different time, new generations have arisen. and we face new challenges. But when we look at the world today, we see similar challenges as which preceded the founding of the United Nations. We see that the international legal order is under pressure in more and more places, even though it is a very foundation to our freedom and prosperity. We see the unending human suffering in Gaza, Sudan, and so many other places in the world. We see violations of international law and of human rights which are in stark contrast to the UN's aims. And we see institutions being undermined, institutions that were established to protect people and populations. And we must not be naive about the causes. These constant threats and attempts to dismantle the legal order are fueled by people and groups with their own agenda. An agenda that runs counter to the interest of everyone else. Yes, everyone. And even those who don't feel directly threatened because they think it doesn't affect them. Sooner or later, everyone is affected, as we saw in the time before the United Nations. And when major powers choose to pursue only their own interest, it is tempting to respond defensively. But as Mahatma Gandhi taught us, an eye for an eye will only make the whole world blind. And so it is time for us, the global community, to choose to pursue the common interest, not by trying to build an entirely new world order, but simply by working together. And the middle powers must take the lead in fostering such international cooperation. And everyone must be able to participate, including those countries who are currently too often left on the sidelines. It is time that countries in Africa, Asia, and Latin America had a fully fledged place, not only on the equal earth map, but in the real world too. To start with, here in the UN, improved African representation in the Security Council at the very least, because If we want to preserve the UN for the future, we must change the balance of power in line with the changing times and modernize our institutions.
